25  Transforms

How do you plot a number your table does not hold? A transform computes it for you and hands the result to a mark. It runs after the table is read and before anything is drawn, and the mark stays what it is: bar * bin still draws bars.

The family has other names. ggplot2 says stat, and the chapter Wilkinson devotes to it says statistics (Wilkinson, 2005); SQL says aggregate, dplyr says summarize, a spreadsheet says pivot. Each of those covers about half of what gog groups here. mean, count and density really are statistics, and they replace rows with a summary. But bin cuts an axis into cells. bounds reshapes two columns you already have and computes nothing at all. stack, dodge, jitter and repel are about collisions between marks rather than about the values behind them. Calling all of that a statistic would misname most of it, so the word here is the most general one that is still accurate: a transform is anything that changes what reaches the mark.

Transforms are applied with the * operator:

mark * transform

The result is the same mark drawing derived values, not a new atom to memorize.

Transform What it does
bin cuts a continuous axis into equal-width cells, and counts the rows in each
smooth fits a LOESS curve (locally weighted regression) through the (x, y) pairs
straight fits the least-squares line through the (x, y) pairs
count counts the rows at each distinct x
density estimates the distribution of x with a Gaussian kernel
proportion divides the measurement by its total, so the shares sum to 1
sum totals y within each x
mean averages y within each x
median the middle y within each x
max the largest y within each x
min the smallest y within each x
quantile the y at one probability within each x, quantile(0.9)
cumulative adds each position’s measurement to the ones before it: the running total
range a band of y per group, as a pair; the whole group, or two quantiles you name
confidence the mean’s confidence interval per group: low, high and center
deviation the spread of y per group: the mean plus and minus a standard deviation
smooth_band the confidence band of smooth’s curve: low, high and center along it
straight_band the confidence band of straight’s line: low, high and center along it

The middle six (sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile) form the aggregation family. All share the same pattern: group by x, reduce y to one value. range, confidence and deviation group the same way but write a low and a high, the extents an interval spans. smooth_band and straight_band write the same pair along a fitted curve and a fitted line. These five and bounds, which comes later in this chapter, are the pair transforms.

Some transforms write their result into a new column, such as count or name, that your table never held. A sentence can name that column, and Columns a transform writes lists every one.

25.1 One variable, or two?

Grouping the transforms by what they compute is not the only useful way to sort them. Seventeen of them also fall into two families by how many columns they read, and reading one column or two is what decides whether you write y(). The other ten of the kernel’s twenty-seven transforms come later in this chapter. bounds reshapes rather than computes. partition, flow, layout and cluster each compute a whole picture, such as a mosaic or a network. dodge, stack, jitter and repel move marks that would otherwise overlap. cumulative adds up a measurement that another transform or a column supplies.

Counting transforms (bin, count, density) supply their own measurement: no column of your table holds it. Given a single variable, they show how its rows are spread. bin and count tally the rows in each bin or category. density estimates the same spread as a smooth curve, whose height is a density rather than a number of rows. proportion joins them when no other transform is written with it, because then the only measurement it has to rescale is the tally it computes itself. You name only the variable whose shape you are asking about, and the transform writes the y column and labels its axis (“Count”, “Proportion”, “Density”). bar * bin + x(life) and line * density + x(life) are the same grammatical shape: one name in, a new axis out. Leaving out y() here is not a mistake. There is exactly one sensible y, the count or the density, and the engine supplies it. If you name a column of the table on that axis, as in bar * count + x(continent) + y(life), gog refuses it, because the transform would never read that column. gog refuses any name except the transform’s own (The name on a measure axis).

Reading transforms (smooth, straight, sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile, range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band) read two columns and summarize the second as it varies with the first. They fit or aggregate an existing y, so you must bind one: without y(gold), bar * mean + x(country) has no way to guess which column to average. Leave y() off and the engine does not guess: only you know which column was meant, so it stops and names what is missing (add y(<column>)). range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band and straight_band are the five that read a y like the others but write more than one: range a low and a high, the other four a low, high and center.

So whether you write y() is not an arbitrary rule to memorize for each transform. The family a transform belongs to decides it. This is one instance of Explicit Over Implicit: the short form is allowed exactly when it cannot be misread, and refused when it could.

Both families replace your rows with a summary of them, and this chapter calls any transform that does so a statistic. A statistic runs within each group when a channel that splits the rows into groups is bound: color, group, pattern or shape. bar * bin + color(species) draws one histogram per species, not one combined bar that has discarded the split (see overlaid histograms). The same rule gives a density curve, a count, or a mean per group. Each output row keeps the group it came from. The mark colors it by that group, and the legend lists the same groups.

25.2 bin: histogram

The first question to ask of one continuous column is how its values are spread. Where are they dense, where are they sparse, and is there one peak or two?

bin is the first counting transform. It cuts x into equal-width bins and counts the rows in each. Combine it with bar to draw a histogram:

gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295
Algeria Africa 2007 72.301 33333216 6223.3675
Angola Africa 2007 42.731 12420476 4797.2313
Argentina Americas 2007 75.320 40301927 12779.3796
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Histogram of life expectancy, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life.”

bin is not the bar’s own transform. Four other marks cut the same bins, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by bin Shape
point * bin one dot at the top of each bin
line * bin the frequency polygon: straight lines through the bin centers
area * bin the same polygon, filled to the baseline
step * bin the staircase outline
bar * bin filled bars, the histogram above

zone * bin cuts two axes instead of one, which is the heatmap, and surface * bin raises the same cells into the cube.

Bin count defaults to Sturges’ rule (Sturges, 1926): k = ⌈log₂(n)⌉ + 1, where n is the number of rows and k the number of bins. In words, each time the number of rows doubles, the histogram gets one more bin. Notice there is no y() in the expression: bin writes the count column itself, and the y axis is labeled “Count” automatically.

25.2.1 Choosing the bin count

A histogram’s shape depends on how it is cut, and the default cut may hide a gap or split a peak. You will often want a finer cut, or bins whose width means something in the data’s units.

Sturges’ rule is a sensible default, not a mandate. Pass a number to set the bin count, or name a width to fix the bin width in the data’s own units:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(30) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin(30)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Thirty bins: a finer histogram"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin into 30, x is life.”

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin(width = 5) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Bins five years wide")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin({ width: 5 })), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("Bins five years wide"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin at width 5, x is life.”

The positional number is the count: bin(30) is thirty bins. A width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, bin(width = 5); the two are mutually exclusive. gog refuses bin(30, width = 5) rather than guess which one you meant. For the same reason a bare number always means a count: on this data, five bins and bins five years wide are very different plots.

A width also decides where the bins start: every edge is a multiple of the width. The five-year bins above therefore run from 35 to 40, from 40 to 45, and so on, not from the smallest value, 39.6. Where the bin edges fall explains why, and how ggplot2 places its edges instead.

25.2.2 Choosing a width

When you give a count of bins, you decide only how much detail to show: bin(20) draws fewer, wider bars than bin(30) on any column. When you give a width, you decide more, because a width is measured in the column’s own units. Use a width when each bin should cover a span that means something, such as five years of life expectancy or half a centimeter of petal length. Because every edge is a multiple of the width, two histograms cut at the same width share their edges, even when their data cover different ranges. You can then compare them bin by bin.

To choose a width, first decide roughly how many bars you want. Divide the column’s range, its largest value minus its smallest, by that number. Then take a nearby round number in the column’s units, such as 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5 or 10. Life expectancy runs from 39.6 to 82.6 years, a range of 43. Ten bars would each be 4.3 years wide, and the nearest round number is 5.

One more rule prevents tall bars and empty bins that come from the cut rather than from the data. The width should be a whole multiple of the distance between two neighboring values the column can hold. quakes_fiji holds a thousand earthquakes near Fiji, and it records each magnitude to one decimal place, so its possible values are 4.0, 4.1, 4.2 and so on, 0.1 apart:

quakes_fiji: first 5 of 1000 rows
east north elevation magnitude slab
181.62 -20.42 -562 4.8 540-630 km
181.03 -20.62 -650 4.2 630-720 km
184.10 -26.00 -42 5.4 0-90 km
181.66 -17.97 -626 4.1 540-630 km
181.96 -20.42 -649 4.0 630-720 km

A width of 0.25 is not a whole multiple of 0.1. Its bins alternate between three possible values and two, so a bin with three collects more earthquakes for that reason alone:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.25) + x(magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.25: bins of three and two values")
(data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.25) + x(col.magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.25: bins of three and two values"))
data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.25) + x(:magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.25: bins of three and two values")
plot(data(quakes_fiji), layer(bar, bin({ width: 0.25 })),
  x(col.magnitude), x_label("Magnitude"),
  title("Width 0.25: bins of three and two values"))

The bar from 4.5 to 4.75 is far taller than the bars on either side. It holds 4.5, 4.6 and 4.7, while each neighbor holds two: 4.3 and 4.4 before it, 4.8 and 4.9 after it. A width of 0.2 puts two possible values in every bin, and the shape is smooth:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin")
(data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(col.magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin"))
data(quakes_fiji) + bar * bin(width = 0.2) + x(:magnitude) +
  x_label("Magnitude") + title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin")
plot(data(quakes_fiji), layer(bar, bin({ width: 0.2 })), x(col.magnitude),
  x_label("Magnitude"), title("Width 0.2: two values in every bin"))

The same rule applies when you give a number of bins, because the number sets the width. Suppose a column holds whole numbers from 9 to 35, so only 27 values are possible. Thirty bins are each 0.87 wide, and at least three must stay empty. For one bar per value, use bar * count, which counts the rows at each value instead of binning them.

Two kinds of axis treat a width differently. A time axis refuses a width, as What a time axis refuses shows, so give the number of bins there. On a log axis the bins are cut on the logarithms, so a width counts powers of the base. In the default base 10, bin(width = 1) makes bins from 100 to 1,000 and from 1,000 to 10,000. In base 2, each bin ends at twice its start.

25.2.3 Why bar * bin, not a histogram() shortcut?

Because bin does the same computation regardless of the mark, and the mark decides how the bins are drawn. bar * bin fills bars. line * bin connects the bin centers into a frequency polygon, and step * bin traces the histogram as a staircase outline. Add stack and a fourth reading appears, the dot plot further down this chapter: one dot per observation rather than one mark per bin. Adding a histogram() shortcut would violate Law 2 (No Exceptions) by special-casing a particular mark+transform pair.

25.2.4 The same bin, cutting two axes

All twelve gapminder years on one scatter make 1704 points, and where they overlap you cannot see how dense the points are. The answer is to count rows in cells of the plane, not only along one axis.

The mark decides something else too: how many axes get cut. Each mark above leaves one axis free to measure the count along, so bin cuts the other one. A zone measures nothing by length, and it needs an extent on both axes to be a rectangle. So the same word cuts both, and the count goes to color, the only channel left holding a number:

gm_all: first 5 of 1704 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 1952 28.801 8425333 779.4453
Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530
Afghanistan Asia 1962 31.997 10267083 853.1007
Afghanistan Asia 1967 34.020 11537966 836.1971
Afghanistan Asia 1972 36.088 13079460 739.9811
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One bin, two axes: the heatmap")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One bin, two axes: the heatmap"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(24) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("One bin, two axes: the heatmap")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(24)), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("One bin, two axes: the heatmap"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 24, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

That is a heatmap, with no atom added to the kernel.

25.2.5 One of each: the mixed mesh

Five continents make five histograms, and comparing five panels is harder than comparing five rows of one picture.

The rule that a zone cuts both axes needs one qualification. What bin cuts is every axis that has a width to cut, and a categorical axis has none, because it arrived already cut: a category is a cell. Give a zone one of each and the transform does the only coherent thing, which is to cut the continuous axis and not the categorical one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(life) + y(continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(col.life) + y(col.continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20) + x(:life) + y(:continent) +
  palette("viridis") + title("One axis cut, one already cut")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20)), x(col.life), y(col.continent),
  palette("viridis"), title("One axis cut, one already cut"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20, x is life, y is continent, with the viridis palette.”

Each continent gets a row of cells, and every row is cut on the same edges, so you can compare the continents by reading straight down. It is a distribution per category shown as shade rather than as height, which is why five of them fit where one histogram would go. The Zone chapter explains this plot, the heatmap and the tile plot below with one rule.

25.2.6 Which mesh: tiling

bin also decides the shape of the cells it cuts, because a different mesh puts different rows in different cells and so changes the counts. Rectangles are the default. Hexagons stagger alternate rows, so a reader does not mistake the straight rows of the mesh for a pattern in the data (Carr et al., 1987):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")
(data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex"))
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(20, tiling = "hex") + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(zone, bin(20, { tiling: "hex" })),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Carr's staggered mesh: tiling = hex"))

“Given all the gapminder years: zones derived by bin into 20 on hexagons, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

A tiling means nothing to a bin that cuts one axis, since there the cells are intervals and an interval has no shape, so bar * bin(tiling = ) is refused pointing at zone. The Zone chapter works through both meshes, including why an empty cell is left unpainted.

25.3 count: frequency aggregation

The first question to ask of a categorical column is how many rows fall in each category. A table with one row per country does not hold that number anywhere.

count counts the number of rows for each unique value of x, and it works on both categorical and continuous columns. It is the categorical counterpart to bin: bin groups a continuous column; count groups a categorical one.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
# How many countries are in each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  title("Countries per continent, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  title("Countries per continent, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent.”

count is not the bar’s own transform. Five other marks tally the same rows, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by count Shape
point * count one dot at each count
line * count the counts joined into a profile
area * count the same profile, filled to the baseline
step * count each count held flat across its slot
zone * count one cell per pair of categories, colored by its count
bar * count one bar per category, the plot above

Compare these bars with the histogram at the start of the chapter. Histogram bars touch, because the bins are cut from one continuous axis and no value falls between them. Bar chart bars are drawn with a gap between them, because the categories are separate.

Like bin, count writes its own y column and labels the axis “Count”. To title that axis yourself, use y_label().

25.3.1 The same count, tallying two axes

With two categorical columns the question becomes how often each pair occurs, such as how many winds came from the west in winter.

bin cuts one axis on a bar and two on a zone, and count works the same way, for the same reason. A bar has a length to show the tally along, so it groups by one axis; a zone measures nothing by length, so it tallies rows into the cell where two categories cross and the count goes to color:

winds: first 5 of 264 rows
direction bearing speed season
N 19.612260 10.1 Winter
N 357.049499 11.0 Winter
N 349.709737 13.8 Winter
N 2.602499 7.4 Winter
N 338.210715 3.7 Summer
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone * count + x(direction) + y(season) +
  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot")
(data(winds) + zone * count + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) +
  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot"))
data(winds) + zone * count + x(:direction) + y(:season) +
  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot")
plot(data(winds), layer(zone, count), x(col.direction), y(col.season),
  title("One count, two axes: the tile plot"))

That is the tile plot (a confusion matrix is the same sentence with different columns), and like the heatmap, no atom was added to the kernel.

Together, bin and count state the whole rule: bin cuts, count tallies. A continuous axis has to be cut into cells before there is anything to count in; a categorical axis arrives already cut, because a category is a cell. So on a zone each is refused where the other belongs, and each refusal names the other.

Taking the two axes one at a time gives three plots, not two. Cut both axes and it is the heatmap; cut neither and it is the tile plot; cut one of two and it is the mixed mesh above. A bin is refused only where there is nothing left for it to cut at all.

25.4 proportion: relative frequency

Fifty-two of the 142 countries are in Africa, and that fact reads differently as a count than as a share of the whole.

proportion divides a measurement by its total and writes shares in [0, 1] that sum to 1. In statistics they are called relative frequencies. Used on its own it has nothing to divide yet, so it tallies the rows first exactly as count does:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
# What share of countries belongs to each continent?
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Continent share, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Continent share, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, x is continent.”

The same six marks read a share as they read a count:

Mark derived by proportion Shape
point * proportion one dot at each share
line * proportion the shares joined into a profile
area * proportion the same profile, filled to the baseline
step * proportion each share held flat across its slot
zone * proportion one cell per pair of categories, colored by its share
bar * proportion one bar per category, the plot above

Use proportion when you care about relative composition rather than raw counts, for example “what fraction of respondents chose each option?” count and proportion differ only by a constant factor, which is the total. So order works the same on both: order(count) after count and order(proportion) after proportion give the same order. Here the bars are horizontal, with the largest share at the top:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + y(continent) +
  order(proportion, desc = TRUE) +
  title("Continent share, largest first")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + y(col.continent) +
  order(col.proportion, desc = True) +
  title("Continent share, largest first"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * proportion + y(:continent) +
  order(:proportion, desc = true) +
  title("Continent share, largest first")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, proportion), y(col.continent),
  order(col.proportion, { desc: true }),
  title("Continent share, largest first"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by proportion, y is continent, ordered by proportion, largest first.”

To sort by the shares, name the column the transform writes, proportion. A column of numbers from your table, such as gdp, is refused in order() after proportion, as Your table’s columns after a transform explains.

proportion also works on two axes, as count does, so zone * proportion reads a tile plot as shares (see Zone).

25.4.1 The total is the whole plot, always

Once a second column splits the bars, each segment could be a share of its own bar or of the whole plot.

The denominator is every row the plot draws, in every context. That is the one thing the word is allowed to mean. Split the bars by a second column and they still sum to 1 between them, so each bar reads as this pair’s share of everything:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(direction) + color(season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations")
(data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(col.direction) + color(col.season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations"))
data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(:direction) + color(:season) +
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations")
plot(data(winds), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.direction),
  color(col.season),
  title("Every bar is a share of all 264 observations"))

“Given the winds: bars derived by proportion, x is direction, color by season.”

Add up the sixteen segments there and you get 1, not 2. What you cannot get that way is the conditional reading: “of the summer winds, what share came from the west”. That reading is the facet. It cuts the data into panels before any of this runs, so each panel normalizes inside itself:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(direction) | facet(season)
data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(col.direction) | facet(col.season)
data(winds) + bar * proportion + x(:direction) | facet(:season)
plot(data(winds), layer(bar, proportion), x(col.direction),
  across(col.season))

“Given the winds: bars derived by proportion, x is direction, split into panel columns by season.”

Compare the two plots. In the first, summer’s bars and winter’s bars share one total. In the second, each season has its own.

25.4.2 Normalizing something other than a tally

Two histograms from tables of different sizes cannot be compared by their counts, and a continent’s population means more as a share of the world’s.

Because proportion divides whatever measurement it finds, it composes with any transform that leaves one number per cell. Put it after a bin and the histogram’s own counts come back as fractions, the relative-frequency histogram, on exactly the mesh a plain bar * bin cuts:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(life) +
  title("Shares, not counts")
(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(col.life) +
  title("Shares, not counts"))
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * proportion + x(:life) +
  title("Shares, not counts")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(20), proportion), x(col.life),
  title("Shares, not counts"))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20 and proportion, x is life.”

Put it after a summary and each slot reads as its share of the grand total. y(population) still names the column that sum adds up. The axis shows shares, so it is titled Proportion:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(continent) + y(population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) +
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population),
  title("Each continent's share of world population, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population.”

proportion writes the shares to a column called proportion, as it does after bin. A text layer with the same two transforms can print each share on its bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(col.proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + text * sum * proportion +
  label(:proportion, decimals = 2) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), layer(text, sum, proportion),
  label(col.proportion, { decimals: 2 }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each continent's share, printed on its bar"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population, and also text derived by sum and proportion, label by proportion with 2 decimal places, with nudge up.”

Asia’s bar is labeled 0.61, about three fifths of the world’s population in 2007. Oceania’s share is 0.0039, so at two decimal places its label reads 0.00.

The text layer’s rows hold two columns. proportion holds each continent’s share, and population still holds the column that sum adds up. So label(population, short = TRUE) prints each continent’s population on its bar, with M for millions and B for billions (a thousand millions), as in Text:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(population, short = TRUE) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  text * sum * proportion + label(col.population, short = True) +
  style(nudge = "up") + title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * proportion + x(:continent) +
  y(:population) + text * sum * proportion +
  label(:population, short = true) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, proportion), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), layer(text, sum, proportion),
  label(col.population, { short: true }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each continent's share, labeled with its population"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and proportion, x is continent, y is population, and also text derived by sum and proportion, label by population written short, with nudge up.”

Asia’s bar reaches 0.61, and its label reads 3.81B, the population of Asia in 2007.

proportion refuses a transform that leaves it nothing to divide by. A density already integrates to 1, and its cells are sample points rather than parts of a whole. A smooth gives a value at each x, so the sum of those values has no meaning. A pair transform writes a low and a high, which leaves two numbers per cell, and a span is not part of any total.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(life)
data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(col.life)
data(gm_all) + line * density * proportion + x(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, density, proportion), x(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `line * density * proportion` has nothing to normalize — a density already integrates to 1, and its cells are points where the estimate was sampled rather than parts of a whole, so the sum of its heights is not a quantity anything is a share of. For the estimated shape, `line * density + x(<number>)`; for shares of the rows themselves, cut them into cells first: `bar * bin * proportion + x(<number>)` is the same curve's histogram, read as fractions.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

25.5 density: kernel density estimate

A histogram’s outline changes with every choice of bin, and its steps belong to the bins rather than to the data. A smooth curve describes the same distribution without the steps.

density is the third counting transform: it estimates the same distribution that bin counts, but as a smooth curve. The curve is the probability density function of x, estimated with a Gaussian kernel and evaluated at 256 evenly spaced points. By default the bandwidth (how wide each kernel is, and so how smooth the curve) is chosen automatically by Silverman’s rule (Silverman, 1986), which uses the interquartile range so that a few extreme values do not widen it.

Combine it with line to draw a smooth density curve:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Kernel density: life expectancy, 2007"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is life.”

density is not the line’s own transform. Five other marks estimate the same curve, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by density Shape
area * density the curve filled to the baseline
step * density the curve as a staircase
point * density one dot at each point the curve was estimated
bar * density one thin bar at each of those points
ribbon * density the curve mirrored, which is the violin
line * density the curve as a stroke, the plot above

Bind two positions instead of one and density cuts both axes. zone then draws the field as cells, path as contour rings, and surface as a sheet.

With one position, as with the other counting transforms, you leave out y(): the transform writes the density column and labels its axis for you.

25.5.1 Choosing the bandwidth

The automatic curve can be smoother than the data supports, hiding a second peak, or rougher, showing bumps that are only noise.

The automatic bandwidth is a sensible default, not a mandate, and it is the parameter you will change most often, as the bin count is for bin. It is set the same two ways. A positional number is an adjust multiplier on the automatic bandwidth: density(2) is twice as smooth, density(0.5) half as smooth and so more jagged.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("density(2): twice as smooth"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(2) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("density(2): twice as smooth")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density(2)), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("density(2): twice as smooth"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density adjusted by 2, x is life.”

To fix the bandwidth in the data’s own units instead, name it. Here bandwidth = 1 sets each kernel one year wide, narrower than the default, so the curve keeps more of the distribution’s fine structure:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(bandwidth = 1) + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ bandwidth: 1 })),
  x(col.life), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("bandwidth = 1 year: an absolute width"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density at bandwidth 1, x is life.”

This works exactly as bin does. The positional number is the adjust multiplier: the common request, since you rarely know the bandwidth you want in advance and only need the automatic one a little smoother or rougher. An absolute width is the less common request, so it is said out loud, density(bandwidth = 1); the two are mutually exclusive, and density(2, bandwidth = 1) refuses with direction rather than guessing which you meant.

25.5.2 A lowest or highest possible value

A density curve continues past the smallest and the largest value, until it is nearly zero at both ends. For most columns that is what you want. Some columns have a lowest possible value, though: no country’s income is below zero. On gdp, the curve then goes below zero, to incomes that no country has:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:gdp) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.gdp),
  x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("No lower limit: the curve goes below zero"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is gdp.”

Write 0 as the axis’s lower limit and leave the upper one missing, limits = c(0, NA) (limits). The curve then starts at 0, and the estimate is corrected there. density places a bell-shaped kernel on each row. The part of a kernel that would fall below zero is mirrored back above it, so near zero the curve is higher than in the plot above:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(gdp, limits = c(0, NA)) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.gdp, limits = [0, None]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:gdp, limits = [0, missing]) +
  x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density),
  x(col.gdp, { limits: [0, null] }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Lower limit 0: the curve starts there"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a line derived by density, x is gdp from 0.”

The curve is now highest at 0, not near 3,000 dollars. Many of the poorest countries lie within one bandwidth of zero, about 4,100 dollars, so their mirrored parts add the most height there.

An upper limit works the same way: limits = c(NA, 1) on a column of shares stops the curve at 1. Only a limit you write does this. When two composed plots share an axis, the range gog chooses for it does not (The marginal plot).

25.5.3 One transform, four readings

Once you have a curve for one column, you will want the same estimate over two columns, or one curve per category, side by side. Each of those is still density.

density estimates a distribution, and how it is drawn depends on what you bind and on the mark. There are four readings, and they are one transform rather than four transforms sharing a name.

Bind one continuous column and it is a curve over that column, with its height on the other axis, which is everything above. Bind two continuous columns to a mark with no measure axis and it is a field over the plane: zone * density paints it cell by cell, and surface * density raises it into the cube. Cut that field into steps of equal density and it becomes a set of levels: path * density traces their edges as contour lines, and zone * density(levels = 8) fills the bands between them. Bind a category and a continuous column and both axes are taken, so the estimate is drawn across the category’s slot, one distribution per group, which is the violin:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(continent) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")
(data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))
data(gapminder_2007) + ribbon * density + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("ribbon * density: the slot reading")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(ribbon, density), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("ribbon * density: the slot reading"))

“Given gapminder 2007: ribbons derived by density, x is continent, y is life.”

This plot draws five estimates, one per continent, and all five are smoothed by the same bandwidth. By default it is the average of the bandwidths Silverman’s rule gives each continent on its own. If each continent kept its own bandwidth, Oceania’s two countries would get one about a ninth of Africa’s, and the two shapes would differ partly because of that. With one bandwidth, a difference in shape comes from the data and not from the smoothing. The same sharing applies whenever one layer draws several estimates: curves split by color, the panels of a facet whose axes are shared, and the frames of an animation made with play. adjust multiplies the shared bandwidth, and a stated bandwidth replaces it.

Split the curve by color, and each continent gets its own curve, smoothed by the same shared bandwidth:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") + title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density + x(:life) + color(:continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density), x(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("line * density + color: one curve per continent"))

“Given gapminder 2007: lines derived by density, x is life, color by continent.”

Each curve encloses the same area, so a continent whose countries are close together draws a tall, narrow curve. Oceania’s two countries are one year apart, so its curve is the tallest. With its own, much smaller bandwidth, it would be nearly three times as tall, and the other four curves would be pressed down against the axis.

Each of density’s parameters belongs to one of the four readings, and gog refuses a parameter in a reading where it has no meaning, rather than ignoring it. bandwidth is a length in one column’s units, so it means nothing to a field, whose two axes measure different quantities. levels counts lines of equal density, and a curve has none to count. The slot reading has two parameters of its own. compare says what a violin’s width means from one slot to the next. reach says how far the shape extends, measured in slots, and past half a slot the shapes reach into their neighbors: the ridgeline. Neither means anything to a plot with no slots:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(life)
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(col.life)
data(gapminder_2007) + line * density(compare = "count") + x(:life)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(line, density({ compare: "count" })),
  x(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `density(compare = )` says what a violin's width means from one slot to the next, and `line * density` here has no slots — it estimates one curve along one axis. Bind a category to give it slots to compare: `ribbon * density(compare = "count") + x(<category>) + y(<number>)`. Otherwise drop `compare`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

25.6 What bin, density and smooth refuse

A histogram of continent is an easy thing to ask for, and gog refuses it. smooth, which fits a trend line, has its own section later in this chapter; it is included here because it is refused for the same reason as bin and density. The refusal is easier to act on once you know what these three transforms share.

One variable, or two? sorted the transforms by how many columns they read. A second property divides them a different way: these three all describe how values are spread along an axis, so the axis they read has to carry a number. A category is one slot rather than a stretch of line, so there is nothing to cut into intervals, nothing for a curve to spread over, and nothing to fit through.

The violin above looks like an exception, but it is not one. There the category is not the axis being estimated along: y(life) is, and the category only says which rows each estimate is made from. Take the number away and there is nothing left to spread over, so the refusal returns. That is why the first two examples below bind a category and nothing else.

Each refusal names the atom that asks the same question of categories. Binning one is really counting it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:continent)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.continent))
Error:
! gog: `bin` cuts a continuous axis into intervals, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a category is one slot, with no width to cut. To tally rows per category, `count` is the transform that does it: `bar * count`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A density over categories is really a share of the total:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(col.continent)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * density + x(:continent)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, density), x(col.continent))
Error:
! gog: `density` estimates a continuous distribution, and `x(continent)` is categorical — there is no number line for the curve to spread along. For the share of rows in each category, that is `bar * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

And a curve fitted across categories is really a summary within each one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * smooth + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, smooth), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve of `y` against `x`, and `x(continent)` is categorical — a fit needs a number line to run along. For a typical value per category, `bar * mean` (or `point * mean`) says it directly.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

Which axis must be continuous is taken from the bindings rather than fixed to x. The horizontal histogram is bar * bin + y(life): it cuts y, because y is the axis it was given, and the count it writes goes on x. smooth is the strict one of the three, since it fits y against x and so needs a number on both.

25.6.1 A fit needs rows to fit through

It is easy to ask for a trend through very few rows: a table filtered to its latest years, or a group with two members.

Having numbers is not the same as having enough of them. smooth fits a curve, and two points are a straight line while one is a point, so it asks for at least three. The two_readings table holds France’s rows for 2002 and 2007, the last two years of the gapminder data:

two_readings: all 2 rows
country continent year life population gdp
France Europe 2002 79.590 59925035 28926.03
France Europe 2007 80.657 61083916 30470.02
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(two_readings) + line * smooth + x(year) + y(life)
data(two_readings) + line * smooth + x(col.year) + y(col.life)
data(two_readings) + line * smooth + x(:year) + y(:life)
plot(data(two_readings), layer(line, smooth), x(col.year), y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and needs at least 3 of them. This data has 2. Plot what you have with `point` and no transform, which draws the rows as rows rather than as a curve through them.

The count that matters is the count inside each group, not in the table. A statistic runs within every group you split by, and faceting splits the rows before any of that. So a table with plenty of rows can still be asked for a fit through two. The recent table holds every country’s rows for 2002 and 2007:

recent: first 5 of 284 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 2002 42.129 25268405 726.7341
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803
Albania Europe 2002 75.651 3508512 4604.2117
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295
Algeria Africa 2002 70.994 31287142 5288.0404
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(recent) + line * smooth + x(year) + y(life) + group(country) |
  facet(continent)
(data(recent) + line * smooth + x(col.year) + y(col.life) + group(col.country) |
  facet(col.continent))
data(recent) + line * smooth + x(:year) + y(:life) + group(:country) |
  facet(:continent)
plot(data(recent), layer(line, smooth), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  group(col.country), across(col.continent))
Error:
! gog: `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and needs at least 3 of them. Split by `continent` or `country`, the smallest group has 2. Drop the split so the fit reads the rows together, or plot what you have with `point` and no transform, which draws the rows as rows rather than as a curve through them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

There are 284 rows there and gog still refuses, because each country in each panel is its own fit and each has only two rows. The message names both splits, so you know which one to remove. Drop group(country) and each panel fits one curve through a continent’s rows, and every continent has more than the three rows a fit needs.

The refusal matters because of what the plot would show without it. Below three rows the curve cannot be computed, so what would be drawn is the rows themselves, connected in order. A two-point group would draw a straight segment beside a hundred-point curve, with nothing to say that one is a fit and the other is the data. An unfinished plot that looks finished is worse than a refusal.

25.7 Chaining transforms

Some questions need two transforms. To show life expectancy across income bands, cut income into bands and take a mean of life inside each one.

Two transforms on one mark have to divide the work, and there are only four jobs to divide. A transform can say where the cells are, it can say what is in them, it can say what scale the answer is read on, and it can say where the marks are drawn. bounds names where each band starts and ends. count tallies into the cells your categories already own, and says nothing about where those cells are. mean and its five siblings reduce a column you name, and say nothing about where the cells are either. proportion does the third job and only the third: it divides by a total, which is why it can come after almost anything. dodge, stack and jitter do the fourth, moving marks that would otherwise land on top of one another. repel also moves labels off one another, but it does no job: it moves a label after every job has run, so it contradicts no other transform. Several of these transforms, mean, bounds and the four that move marks among them, have their own sections later in this chapter. Here they appear only as examples of how two transforms combine.

Two transforms compose when they do different jobs, and contradict when they do the same one. A cell holds one extent, one measurement, one scale and one place for its marks. A second transform doing a job the first already did therefore leaves no reading that keeps both. The engine refuses, rather than drawing one and quietly discarding the other. Combinations has the whole grid, generated from the same rule.

Because each job is filled once, the order you write them in does not change the picture. Still, write them in the order they are computed, so the sentence reads in the same order as the work.

bin does two of the four jobs, and it is the only transform that can drop one of them. Cutting an axis is what makes it a bin; the tally it hands back is a by-product of the cut. So when you compose it with another statistic, bin keeps the cut and the other statistic keeps the measurement. The plot uses the gm_all table, shown in The same bin, cutting two axes:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band")
(data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band"))
data(gm_all) + bar * bin(20) * mean + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin(20), mean),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  title("Mean life expectancy by income band"))

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by bin into 20 and mean, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

Read the sentence as three separate claims. bin(20) cuts income into twenty bands. mean reduces life within each one. bar draws the result as a length from zero. The bars touch because the bands tile the axis, exactly as a histogram’s do, and the y axis is now labeled for the column that was actually reduced.

Any mark that accepts both transforms accepts the pair. Here the same cut is drawn as points, with median in place of mean:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  title("Median life expectancy by income band")
(data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  title("Median life expectancy by income band"))
data(gm_all) + point * bin(20) * median + x(:gdp, scale = "log") +
  y(:life) + title("Median life expectancy by income band")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin(20), median),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  title("Median life expectancy by income band"))

“Given all the gapminder years: points derived by bin into 20 and median, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life.”

25.7.1 What cannot be chained, and why

Having seen bin * mean work, you will want to know which other pairs do.

The other two counting transforms cannot drop their measurement, because measuring is all they do. Take it away from count and nothing is left of it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gm_all) + bar * count * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, mean), x(col.continent), y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bar * count * mean` measures each cell twice — `count` supplies only a measurement: its cells are the slots the positions already own, so with `mean` measuring them too the cell is measured twice and `count` has nothing left to contribute. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * count` to measure what `count` computes, or `bar * mean` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

density fails a different test. Its cells are the points where the estimate was sampled, and the estimate exists between your observations rather than inside cells that hold rows, so there is nothing inside one for a statistic to reduce:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(gdp) + y(life)
data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
data(gm_all) + bar * density * mean + x(:gdp) + y(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, density, mean), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bar * density * mean` measures each cell twice — a `density` cell is a point where the estimate was sampled, not a bucket holding rows — the estimate exists *between* your observations — so there is nothing inside one for `mean` to reduce. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * density` to measure what `density` computes, or `bar * mean` to reduce the column you name. To cut a continuous axis into cells and reduce a column inside each, `bin` is the transform that cuts without keeping the measurement: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

smooth is refused against all three, including bin, for a reason none of them share. It fits a curve through the rows and already averages locally while it fits, so cutting them into cells first asks the same question a second time:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(gdp) + y(life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * smooth + x(:gdp) + y(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin, smooth), x(col.gdp), y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * smooth` asks one question twice — `smooth` fits a curve through the rows and already averages locally as it goes, so cutting them into cells first changes nothing it was not doing. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * smooth + x(<a>) + y(<b>)` for the fitted curve, or `bar * bin` for the shape `bin` measures. For a summary per cell rather than a fitted curve, name the statistic: `bar * bin * mean + x(<a>) + y(<b>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

And two transforms that each write their own measurement are the same contradiction. bin gives up its tally only to a transform that reduces a column you named, and count reads none, so a cell would be measured twice:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(col.life)
data(gm_all) + bar * bin * count + x(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, bin, count), x(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `bar * bin * count` measures each cell twice — `bin` and `count` each invent their own measurement from the rows, and neither was handed a column to give way to, so there is no reading that keeps both. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * bin` or `bar * count`. To cut an axis into cells and measure something else inside them, the second transform has to be one you hand a column: `bar * bin * mean + x(<number>) + y(<column>)`. To read either as shares of the whole rather than as counts, `proportion` rescales whichever you keep: `bar * bin * proportion`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

Each refusal names both transforms you could drop. Each also names a third option, bar * bin * mean, because bin is the one transform that cuts without keeping its measurement.

The same rule applies to transforms that write a low and a high, and to the transforms that move marks. Two transforms that both write a low and a high measure the cell twice. So range and confidence cannot be used together. A minimum and a maximum are not a 95% confidence interval, and one of the two would have to be discarded:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gm_all) + interval * range * confidence + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(interval, range, confidence), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `interval * range * confidence` measures each cell twice — `range` and `confidence` both reduce the column you named, and a cell holds one answer, so drawing both would mean drawing one of them and discarding the other. Keep whichever you meant: `interval * range` or `interval * confidence`. To show both, draw them as two layers: `interval * range + interval * confidence`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The same is true when one transform writes a single value and the other writes two:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(year) + y(population)
data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(col.year) + y(col.population)
data(gm_all) + line * sum * range + x(:year) + y(:population)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, sum, range), x(col.year),
  y(col.population))
Error:
! gog: `line * sum * range` measures each cell twice — `sum` and `range` both reduce the column you named, and a cell holds one answer, so drawing both would mean drawing one of them and discarding the other. Keep whichever you meant: `line * sum` or `line * range`. To show both, draw them as two layers: `line * sum + line * range`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

Two transforms that move marks are the same contradiction on the fourth job. A bar cannot be set beside its neighbor and piled on top of it at once, because a bar can be in only one place:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(continent) + color(continent)
data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(col.continent) + color(col.continent)
data(gm_all) + bar * count * dodge * stack + x(:continent) +
  color(:continent)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, dodge, stack), x(col.continent),
  color(col.continent))
Error:
! gog: `bar * dodge * stack` arranges the same marks twice — `dodge` and `stack` each decide where colliding groups go, and a mark sits in one place, so one of the two would be discarded. Keep whichever you meant: `bar * dodge` or `bar * stack`. To show both readings, draw them as two plots side by side rather than as one layer.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A transform can also be unnecessary rather than contradictory, and that is a different answer. proportion divides a tally by its total, so it already counts the rows, which leaves count beside it with nothing to add. The plot is still exactly the plot you asked for, so the engine draws it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent")
(data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(col.continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent"))
data(gm_all) + bar * count * proportion + x(:continent) +
  title("Share of countries by continent")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(bar, count, proportion), x(col.continent),
  title("Share of countries by continent"))
gog: `bar * count * proportion` draws the same plot as `bar * proportion` — a share is a share *of* a tally, so `proportion` already counts the rows and `count` adds nothing. Drop it, or keep `bar * count` on its own to read the tallies themselves rather than their shares.

“Given all the gapminder years: bars derived by count and proportion, x is continent.”

The note printed with the plot names the shorter sentence, bar * proportion, that draws the same picture.

That is the difference between the two answers. When the two transforms cannot both be used, the engine refuses rather than discard one. When both can stay and one of them simply changes nothing, it draws and says so. Neither answer is silence, which is the rule underneath both: a word you wrote is never read and then ignored.

25.8 smooth: LOESS trend line

The counting transforms read one column and write a new measurement. The reading transforms summarize a measurement you already have: each one reads a column you name, usually on y, and answers with a summary of it. smooth is the first of them.

Income and life expectancy rise together across the scatter, and one curve states that relationship more plainly than 142 separate points.

smooth fits a locally weighted linear regression (LOESS) through the (x, y) points and evaluates it at 100 evenly spaced x positions (Cleveland, 1979). Each local regression is fitted once, with no second fit that gives outliers less weight. The curve is the engine’s own, so it is identical in all four languages.

Combine smooth with line to overlay a trend line on a scatterplot. The plot uses the gapminder_2007 table, shown in the bin section:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * smooth +
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + color(:continent) +
  line * smooth + title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  color(col.continent), layer(line, smooth),
  title("GDP vs life expectancy, with a LOESS smooth"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by smooth.”

smooth is not the line’s own transform. Four other marks fit the same curve, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by smooth Shape
point * smooth one dot at each fitted value
area * smooth the curve filled to the baseline
bar * smooth one thin bar at each fitted value
step * smooth the curve as a staircase
line * smooth the fitted curve above

Span is fixed at 0.75: each local regression uses the nearest 75% of the data. A larger span would give a smoother curve, but smooth takes no argument, so the span cannot be changed. smooth needs continuous columns on x and y, and at least three rows in each group. Both refusals are earlier in this chapter, under What bin, density and smooth refuse. It writes its fitted values under the same x and y names, so the axes keep their labels.

ggplot2’s geom_smooth() uses the same span, 0.75, but differs in two ways. First, its default fit is a local quadratic: a small parabola around each x position, not a straight line. So the two curves can differ where the relationship is curved, most often at their left and right ends. Second, when any group has 1,000 rows or more, geom_smooth() fits a generalized additive model instead of LOESS. In that case, the two curves come from different methods, and the difference can be larger.

25.8.1 smooth_band: the band around the curve

A curve through the points says where the trend lies. A band around it says how precisely the trend is known. confidence adds a low and a high around a mean; smooth_band adds them around smooth’s curve. At the 100 x positions smooth uses, smooth_band writes the curve’s confidence band as a low and a high, with the fitted value as the center. A ribbon fills the band, and line * smooth draws the curve inside it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point +
  ribbon * smooth_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point +
  ribbon * smooth_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + ribbon * smooth_band +
  style(opacity = 0.3) + line * smooth +
  title("The trend, and how precisely it is known")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  layer(ribbon, smooth_band), style({ opacity: 0.3 }),
  layer(line, smooth), title("The trend, and how precisely it is known"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points, and also a ribbon derived by smooth_band, and also a line derived by smooth.”

The band widens at the right, where only a few rich countries lie. Where fewer rows lie near an x position, the trend there is known less precisely. The band shows the uncertainty of the curve, not the spread of the countries, so three countries in four lie outside it. Its center is smooth’s curve exactly. The confidence level is 0.95 unless you name another, and smooth_band(0.99) draws a wider band.

Like smooth, smooth_band needs two continuous columns, but it needs five rows in each group, not three. The band’s width is computed from how far the rows lie from the curve. With three or four rows, the curve passes through every row, so no width can be computed. line * smooth_band draws the band’s two edges instead of filling it.

25.9 straight: the least-squares line

smooth lets its curve bend wherever the points bend. Often you want a simpler answer: one straight line, and how steeply it rises. straight fits the least-squares line: the straight line that makes the sum of the squared vertical distances from the points as small as possible. It is the simple linear regression line, the one R’s lm(y ~ x) fits. gog computes the line itself, so it is the same in all four languages. It draws the line at the same 100 x positions as smooth, which the band below needs, because the band’s edges curve.

Life expectancy does not rise along a straight line with GDP. It rises quickly among the poorest countries and slowly among the richest. Here smooth, in red, and straight, in blue, are fitted to the same countries on a linear axis of dollars:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  point + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "tomato") +
  line * straight + style(color = "steelblue") +
  title("A straight line on dollars misses the bend")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  point + style(color = "lightgray") +
  line * smooth + style(color = "tomato") +
  line * straight + style(color = "steelblue") +
  title("A straight line on dollars misses the bend"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point +
  style(color = "lightgray") + line * smooth + style(color = "tomato") +
  line * straight + style(color = "steelblue") +
  title("A straight line on dollars misses the bend")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  style({ color: "lightgray" }), layer(line, smooth),
  style({ color: "tomato" }), layer(line, straight),
  style({ color: "steelblue" }),
  title("A straight line on dollars misses the bend"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points, and also a line derived by smooth, and also a line derived by straight.”

The curve bends near $10,000 and the straight line cannot. Among the 66 countries under $5,000, the line lies above six in ten. At the richest country it reaches 91 years, about eight years more than the longest life expectancy in the table. So on a linear axis of dollars, a straight line is a poor summary.

Against the logarithm of GDP, the rise is close to a straight line, so the next plot puts x on a log scale. On a log x axis, straight fits the line to the logarithm of x, so the line is straight on the page:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  point + color(continent) +
  line * straight +
  title("Life expectancy against GDP on a log scale")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  point + color(col.continent) +
  line * straight +
  title("Life expectancy against GDP on a log scale"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + point +
  color(:continent) + line * straight +
  title("Life expectancy against GDP on a log scale")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  point, color(col.continent), layer(line, straight),
  title("Life expectancy against GDP on a log scale"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, points colored by continent, and also a line derived by straight.”

The line rises about 16.6 years for each tenfold rise in GDP per person, for example from $1,000 to $10,000. Like smooth, straight fits one line for each group when a channel splits the rows. Here color is written before the marks, so it reaches the line as well as the points:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) + color(continent) +
  point +
  line * straight +
  title("One line for each continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  point +
  line * straight +
  title("One line for each continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  color(:continent) + point + line * straight +
  title("One line for each continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  color(col.continent), point, layer(line, straight),
  title("One line for each continent"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, color by continent, points, and also lines derived by straight.”

Within each continent the lines are flatter: between about 8 and 12 more years for each tenfold rise, compared with 16.6 across all countries. The line across all countries is steeper partly because the continents differ: on the richer continents, people also live longer on average. Oceania has only two countries, so its line passes through both of them.

straight needs continuous columns on x and y, as smooth does. In each group it needs at least two rows, with two different values of x. The refusals for a category on either axis are the ones under What bin, density and smooth refuse. It writes its fitted values under the same x and y names, so the axes keep their labels.

straight has one refusal that smooth does not have. A transform measures y in the column’s own units (The order of a scale and a transform). On a log y axis, a line that is straight in those units would be drawn as a curve. So gog refuses straight on a log y axis:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life, scale = "log") +
  point + line * straight
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life, scale = "log") +
  point + line * straight)
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life, scale = "log") + point +
  line * straight
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life, { scale: "log" }),
  point, layer(line, straight))
Error:
! gog: `line * straight` fits a straight line to `life` in its own units, and a log axis would draw that line as a curve. To fit a line to the logarithm of `life`, take the logarithm in your table and plot it on a linear axis. To keep the log axis, `line * smooth` fits a curve, which may bend.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To fit a line to the logarithm of a column, take the logarithm in your table and plot that column on a linear axis. To keep the log axis, use smooth, whose curve may bend. A log x axis is not refused, because there the line is fitted to the logarithm of x, as the second plot in this section showed.

25.9.1 straight_band: the band around the line

straight_band adds a band around straight’s line, as smooth_band does around smooth’s curve. At each of the line’s 100 x positions, it writes the confidence interval of the line as a low and a high, with the fitted value as the center. The R function predict() gives the same interval for a model from lm(), with interval = "confidence". A ribbon fills the band:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  point +
  ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * straight +
  title("The line, and how precisely it is known")
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  point +
  ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) +
  line * straight +
  title("The line, and how precisely it is known"))
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + point +
  ribbon * straight_band + style(opacity = 0.3) + line * straight +
  title("The line, and how precisely it is known")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life),
  point, layer(ribbon, straight_band), style({ opacity: 0.3 }),
  layer(line, straight), title("The line, and how precisely it is known"))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, points, and also a ribbon derived by straight_band, and also a line derived by straight.”

The band is narrowest at the mean of the x values. On this log axis that is a GDP of about $5,500, where the band is 2.4 years wide. It widens toward both ends: 5.7 years at the poorest country and 4.5 years at the richest. As with smooth_band, the band shows how precisely the line is known, not the spread of the countries, so about three countries in four lie outside it. The confidence level is 0.95 unless you name another, and straight_band(0.99) draws a wider band. The band needs three rows in each group, one more than the line.

25.10 Aggregation family: sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile

The six summaries are the simplest members of the reading family. A table can hold several rows for the same x value, for example medals from different years all labeled “USA”. bar alone then draws one bar per row, and the bars for one country are drawn over each other in one slot.
