The aggregation family groups rows by x and reduces y to a single value per group. All six follow exactly the same grammar:

bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * median + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * max + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * min + x(country) + y(gold)
bar * quantile(0.9) + x(country) + y(gold)

sum, total y per group, the most common aggregation for counts and amounts:

medal_repeats: all 5 rows
country gold
USA 10
USA 5
GBR 8
GBR 4
JPN 6
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Total gold medals") + title("Sum per country: bar * sum")
(data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Total gold medals") + title("Sum per country: bar * sum"))
data(medal_repeats) + bar * sum + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Total gold medals") +
  title("Sum per country: bar * sum")
plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, sum), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Total gold medals"),
  title("Sum per country: bar * sum"))

“Given the medal repeats table: bars derived by sum, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”

sum is not the bar’s own transform, and the whole family behaves alike:

Mark derived by sum Shape
point * sum one dot at each total
line * sum the totals joined into a profile
area * sum the same profile, filled to the baseline
step * sum each total held flat across its slot
zone * sum one cell per pair of categories, colored by its total
bar * sum one bar per category, the plot above

You can put mean, median, min, max or quantile in place of sum in every row of that table. The statistic decides the number, and the mark decides the shape.

mean, average y per group, useful for comparing typical values:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Mean gold medals") + title("Mean per country: bar * mean")
(data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Mean gold medals") + title("Mean per country: bar * mean"))
data(medal_repeats) + bar * mean + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Mean gold medals") +
  title("Mean per country: bar * mean")
plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, mean), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Mean gold medals"),
  title("Mean per country: bar * mean"))

median, the middle value, robust to outliers:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medal_repeats) + bar * median + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Median gold") + title("Median per country: bar * median")
(data(medal_repeats) + bar * median + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Median gold") + title("Median per country: bar * median"))
data(medal_repeats) + bar * median + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Median gold") +
  title("Median per country: bar * median")
plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, median), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Median gold"),
  title("Median per country: bar * median"))

max, the largest value within each group:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medal_repeats) + bar * max + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Max gold") + title("Max per country: bar * max")
(data(medal_repeats) + bar * max + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Max gold") + title("Max per country: bar * max"))
data(medal_repeats) + bar * max + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Max gold") +
  title("Max per country: bar * max")
plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, max), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Max gold"),
  title("Max per country: bar * max"))

“Given the medal repeats table: bars derived by max, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”

min, the smallest value within each group:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medal_repeats) + bar * min + x(country) + y(gold) +
  order(gold, desc = TRUE) +
  y_label("Min gold") + title("Min per country: bar * min")
(data(medal_repeats) + bar * min + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  order(col.gold, desc = True) +
  y_label("Min gold") + title("Min per country: bar * min"))
data(medal_repeats) + bar * min + x(:country) + y(:gold) +
  order(:gold, desc = true) + y_label("Min gold") +
  title("Min per country: bar * min")
plot(data(medal_repeats), layer(bar, min), x(col.country), y(col.gold),
  order(col.gold, { desc: true }), y_label("Min gold"),
  title("Min per country: bar * min"))

“Given the medal repeats table: bars derived by min, x is country, y is gold, ordered by gold, largest first.”

All six aggregations work the same whether x is continuous or categorical. For a categorical x, groups keep the column’s declared order if it has one, and otherwise the order in which they first appear, unless you set one with order. For a continuous x, groups are sorted ascending.

Transform What it computes per group
sum total of y values
mean arithmetic average of y
median middle value of y
max largest y value
min smallest y value
quantile(p) the y at probability p

25.10.1 The same six, grouping by a pair

Mean wind speed by direction is one bar chart. Mean wind speed by direction and season is a grid of cells, with one mean in each.

On a zone, count tallies two axes instead of one, and these six do the same, for the same reason. A bar has a length to show the answer along, so it groups by one position and measures along the other. A zone measures nothing by length. Both its positions are free to be grouping columns, and the answer goes to color. The plot uses the winds table, shown in The same count, tallying two axes:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed) +
  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair")
(data(winds) + zone * mean + x(col.direction) + y(col.season) + color(col.speed) +
  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair"))
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(:direction) + y(:season) + color(:speed) +
  title("The same mean, grouped by a pair")
plot(data(winds), layer(zone, mean), x(col.direction), y(col.season),
  color(col.speed), title("The same mean, grouped by a pair"))

The cells for west are the darkest in both rows: winds from the west average about 21 in summer and in winter alike. Each direction changes little from one season to the other, so on this table the direction a wind comes from says more about its speed than the season does.

The channel that names the column to reduce is also the channel that shows the result. That is not a special case for the zone: a summary reduces in place everywhere, and on bar * mean + x(country) + y(gold) it is y that both names gold and receives the average. A zone measures by color, so there color both names the column and shows the result.

So the whole rule fits in one sentence: a summary groups by every position the mark does not measure with, and reduces the column named on the one it does.

mark positions measures with groups by reduces
bar x, y y x y
bar in space() x, y, z z x, y z
surface x, y, z z x, y z
zone x, y color x, y color

The middle two rows are identical, and that is the rule working rather than a coincidence: a 3-D bar and a surface have the same three positions and measure along the same one, so they group and reduce alike. Only the shape drawn on each (x, y) cell differs: an upright bar, or a flat plateau.

What separates these six from count, bin and density is not the number of axes, since all nine can group by one axis or two. It is whether a column was named for them. Those three supply their own measurement. They need no column named, and they write the answer into a new column. These six are given a column instead, so the sentence has to say which one, and the answer replaces it. proportion after another transform belongs to neither group: it divides the measurement that transform wrote. On its own it counts the rows first, as count does.

25.10.2 Why these names?

The six names follow one rule. sum, mean, median, max, min and quantile each name an operation on y, not a data type and not a chart name. The * operator makes this explicit: bar * sum reads as “a bar that sums”. Every aggregation is the word a statistics course already uses (Law 3: Plain Names).

25.11 quantile: one point in the distribution

sum, mean, median, max and min each answer a fixed question. quantile takes the question as its argument: quantile(0.9) is the value below which nine tenths of the group falls, which is the 90th percentile.

Many reported numbers have exactly that form. A service level is the 95th percentile of response time. A growth chart is a set of percentiles by age. A pay band is usually quoted at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles. Here are three of them across every country, year by year. The plot uses the gm_all table, shown in The same bin, cutting two axes:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + x(year) + y(life) +
  line * quantile(0.9) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th")
(data(gm_all) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  line * quantile(0.9) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th"))
data(gm_all) + x(:year) + y(:life) + line * quantile(0.9) +
  style(color = "steelblue") + line * median + style(color = "gray") +
  line * quantile(0.1) + style(color = "tomato") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th")
plot(data(gm_all), x(col.year), y(col.life), layer(line, quantile(0.9)),
  style({ color: "steelblue" }), layer(line, median),
  style({ color: "gray" }), layer(line, quantile(0.1)),
  style({ color: "tomato" }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The 90th percentile, the median, and the 10th"))

“Given all the gapminder years: x is year, y is life, a line derived by quantile at 0.9, colored steelblue, and also a line derived by median, colored gray, and also a line derived by quantile at 0.1, colored tomato.”

The three lines are three sentences over one table, and they say different things about the same 142 countries. The middle rose steadily. The top rose more slowly, because it was already high. The bottom rose and then declined for a decade, which neither of the others shows.

Each of those three lines named its own probability: 0.9, 0.5 written as median, and 0.1. Leave the probability out and nothing can run, because quantile has no default the way bin and density do. Every other transform whose parameter is a number works bare, and this one is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + line * quantile + x(year) + y(life)
data(gm_all) + line * quantile + x(col.year) + y(col.life)
data(gm_all) + line * quantile + x(:year) + y(:life)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, quantile), x(col.year), y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `quantile` needs the probability it reduces to, e.g. `quantile(0.9)` for the 90th percentile. There is no default, because the only sensible one is the middle and that already has a plain name: `median`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The only sensible default is the middle, and the middle already has a plain name. That is also why three particular values get a warning rather than a refusal:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + line * quantile(0.5) + x(year) + y(life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The median, written as a quantile")
(data(gm_all) + line * quantile(0.5) + x(col.year) + y(col.life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The median, written as a quantile"))
data(gm_all) + line * quantile(0.5) + x(:year) + y(:life) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The median, written as a quantile")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(line, quantile(0.5)), x(col.year), y(col.life),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("The median, written as a quantile"))
gog: `quantile(0.5)` is the median — write `median` for the plain name. Drawn as asked.

The plot draws, and gog says that median is the plain name for it. quantile(0) and quantile(1) say the same about min and max. They are not refused, because a program that draws every decile in turn would then fail at 0.5 for no good reason. They are not silent either, because Orthogonality says no atom is redundant.

25.12 range: a low/high pair

A mean per species says where each group is and nothing about how far its values reach.

The aggregation family writes one measured value per group. range is the first to write two: the minimum and the maximum of y within each group, emitted as a low then a high. That pair is exactly what an interval spans:

iris_flowers: first 5 of 150 rows
sepal_length sepal_width petal_length species
5.1 3.5 1.4 setosa
4.9 3.0 1.4 setosa
4.7 3.2 1.3 setosa
4.6 3.1 1.5 setosa
5.0 3.6 1.4 setosa
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length range per species")
(data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length range per species"))
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range + x(:species) + y(:petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Petal length range per species")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Petal length range per species"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range, x is species, y is petal length.”

range is not the interval’s own transform. Three other marks read the same low and high value, and only the shape changes:

Mark derived by range Shape
ribbon * range the band between the two values, filled
line * range the two values as two separate strokes
step * range the same two boundaries, as staircases
interval * range one whisker per group, the plot above

You can put confidence, deviation or bounds in place of range in every row of that table, and bounds adds zone, which shades the region between its two columns.

range reads a y and groups by x exactly like the aggregation family: it needs a y() and works the same whether x is continuous or categorical. What differs is the output: two rows per group instead of one. This low/high-rows shape is reused elsewhere. The box mark encodes its own summary the same way, with the two whisker ends as the pair of rows and the quartiles alongside. The ribbon mark fills between the same pair as a continuous band. See Interval for the whisker, and for why its extents come from a transform rather than from two extra channels the kernel would never otherwise have.

25.12.1 A band between two quantiles

The minimum and the maximum each come from a single row, so one unusual row moves the whole span. To show the middle of a group instead of its extremes, give range two quantiles:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")
(data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 0.75) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Middle half of petal length per species")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range(0.25, 0.75)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Middle half of petal length per species"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by range from 0.25 to 0.75, x is species, y is petal length.”

The two numbers are quantile probabilities, so range(0.25, 0.75) spans the first quartile to the third. That span is the interquartile range, and it is the same one a box draws as its body, computed by the same rule. Any other pair works the same way: range(0.1, 0.9) keeps the middle 80%, and range(0.05, 0.95) the middle 90%.

Bare range is range(0, 1), because the quantile at 0 is the minimum and the quantile at 1 is the maximum. So interval * range is unchanged, and the two arguments only make its default visible. Naming one end leaves the other at its extreme, so range(high = 0.9) runs from the smallest value to the 90th percentile.

Both ends are probabilities. A number below 0 or above 1 is refused, not corrected:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 75) + x(species) + y(petal_length)
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 75) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length)
data(iris_flowers) + interval * range(0.25, 75) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length)
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, range(0.25, 75)), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length))
Error:
! gog: `range(high = 75)` is not a probability — the band's ends are quantiles, so each is between 0 and 1. `range(0.25, 0.75)` is the middle half, `range(0.1, 0.9)` the middle 80 percent, and bare `range` the whole group.

For a low and a high you computed yourself, in the data’s own units, use bounds instead.

25.13 confidence: the interval of the mean

range shows the full spread of a group. Often the question is the uncertainty of the mean instead, which is what an error bar shows. confidence computes the mean’s confidence interval per group (mean ± t·se, with se the standard error: the t-interval), emitting a low, a high, and a center. That center is what turns the whisker into a pointrange, a whisker with a dot at its center:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")
(data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length"))
data(iris_flowers) + interval * confidence(0.95) + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("95% CI of mean petal length")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, confidence(0.95)),
  x(col.species), y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"),
  y_label("Petal length (cm)"), title("95% CI of mean petal length"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by confidence at 95%, x is species, y is petal length.”

The level is a parameter, exactly like bin(30) and density(2): confidence alone is 95%, confidence(0.99) is wider. It uses the t-distribution (not a fixed 1.96), so a small group’s interval is genuinely wider. A group of one has no spread, and its interval collapses to a point.

The center dot appears because the statistic has a center; range has none, so it draws a bare whisker. That is the rule for every pair transform: the transform decides whether there is a center, and the mark draws what it is given. So the difference between an error bar and a pointrange is which statistic you ask for, not another mark to remember.

25.14 deviation: the spread of the data

confidence says how precisely a mean is known. deviation says how far the values behind it spread. That is a different question, drawn as the same picture: deviation emits the same low, high and center, so it also draws a pointrange:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(species) + y(petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")
(data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(col.species) + y(col.petal_length) +
  x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))
data(iris_flowers) + interval * deviation + x(:species) +
  y(:petal_length) + x_label("Species") + y_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(interval, deviation), x(col.species),
  y(col.petal_length), x_label("Species"), y_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Mean petal length, with one standard deviation"))

“Given the iris flowers: intervals derived by deviation, x is species, y is petal length.”

The number of standard deviations is a parameter, like confidence’s level: deviation alone reaches one standard deviation on each side of the mean, and deviation(2) reaches two, so that band is four standard deviations wide. The standard deviation is the sample one, dividing by n − 1, so a group of one has no spread to show and collapses to a point exactly as confidence does.

Neither transform makes the other redundant, and neither does range. On the iris flowers the confidence band is under a third as long as the deviation band: fifty measurements locate a mean precisely, and their spread stays as wide as it was. Adding rows narrows the first band, while the second stays about as wide as it was. Interval draws the two side by side and says which sentence each one supports.

range(0.25, 0.75) answers a third version of the question. It reads the sorted values, so it reports where the middle half of the values actually lie. deviation starts from the mean instead, and reports a distance out from it. On a skewed group they disagree, and the disagreement is informative rather than a defect.

25.15 bounds: a pre-computed low/high pair

range and confidence compute the pair from raw values. bounds is their counterpart that computes nothing. Sometimes you already have the low and the high in two columns, computed before the plot: a model’s standard error, a psychometric standard error of measurement, a bootstrap interval. bounds(lower, upper) reshapes those two columns into the very same low/high pair, so a ribbon or interval draws them with no new atom and no new rule:

score_band: first 5 of 21 rows
score expected lower upper
0 0 -1.610304 1.610304
1 1 -1.865557 3.865557
2 2 -1.944424 5.944424
3 3 -1.694803 7.694803
4 4 -1.259232 9.259232
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed band: ribbon with bounds")
(data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(col.lower, col.upper) + x(col.score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed band: ribbon with bounds"))
data(score_band) + ribbon * bounds(:lower, :upper) + x(:score) +
  y_label("Expected true score") + x_label("Raw score") +
  title("A pre-computed band: ribbon with bounds")
plot(data(score_band), layer(ribbon, bounds(col.lower, col.upper)),
  x(col.score), y_label("Expected true score"), x_label("Raw score"),
  title("A pre-computed band: ribbon with bounds"))

“Given the score band: a ribbon from lower to upper, x is score.”

It differs from every transform above in two ways that both follow from reshaping, not computing. Its arguments are column names, not a number: it has to be told which columns hold the bounds. And it needs no y(): those two columns are the extents, so (like count, which writes its own y column) the mark takes its low and high from bounds and the y axis fits them. bounds shows where gog stops computing. gog offers a small, deliberate set of statistics; everything else you compute yourself, and bounds draws a band you already have.

It is legal on the five marks that can draw a low/high pair, each a different geometry over the same pair, the No Exceptions rule that lets every mark in the bin table draw the same bins:

  • ribbon fills the pair (a filled band),
  • interval draws a whisker across it at each x,
  • line traces its two boundaries (the unfilled band),
  • step traces them as staircases (stepped control limits), and
  • zone shades the region between them, the band that names its own sides rather than tracking a curve.

So line * bounds(lower, upper) + style(pattern = "dashed") is the unfilled, dashed error band: the two ± curves with no fill between them. It is the same pair that ribbon * bounds fills, drawn by a different mark. gog refuses bounds on any other mark, and the message points to the band marks, or to a summary such as mean for one value per group.

25.16 partition: a whole among nested parts

Nearly every transform so far reads a column and writes a summary of it; bounds alone reshapes what you already had. partition reads a hierarchy: two or three columns that trace the path down to each row. It writes the region each node of that hierarchy occupies, four edges and a center, which is exactly what bin writes for a cell. That is what makes it a transform rather than a coordinate space, and it is why zone needs nothing new to draw the result.

The hierarchy’s levels can run two ways, and the difference is one parameter. Nested is the default: every level divides the same axis, and the other axis adds one band per level. On a flat plot that reading is the icicle. In polar() each band becomes a ring, which is the sunburst, and that chapter works it through in full.

Crossed is the other, and it is the one this chapter draws. The levels alternate: the first divides the width, the second divides the height within each of those columns, a third would divide the width again. The plot it makes is the mosaic.

25.16.1 The mosaic

A cross-tabulation raises two questions at once: how the two categories relate, and how many people each cell counts. A mosaic answers both in one picture.

commutes is a survey of how people get to work in four cities, one row per city and mode, with a count:

commutes: first 6 of 16 rows
city mode people
Ashford Car 980
Ashford Bus or tram 340
Ashford Bicycle 110
Ashford On foot 110
Brightwell Car 420
Brightwell Bus or tram 380
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(commutes) + zone * partition(city, mode, cross = TRUE) + x(people) +
  color(mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("How four cities get to work")
(data(commutes) + zone * partition(col.city, col.mode, cross = True) + x(col.people) +
  color(col.mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("How four cities get to work"))
data(commutes) + zone * partition(:city, :mode, cross = true) +
  x(:people) + color(:mode) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("How four cities get to work")
plot(data(commutes),
  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true })),
  x(col.people), color(col.mode),
  style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  x_label("People surveyed"), title("How four cities get to work"))

“Given the commutes: zones derived by partition through city and mode, crossed, x is people, color by mode.”

Two marks read a partition, and text names the boxes that zone draws:

Mark derived by partition Shape
text * partition the node’s own name, at its center
zone * partition one box per node, the plot above

The plot shows two variables, one in each direction. A column’s width is that city’s share of everyone surveyed, so Ashford’s column is three times Millbrook’s; a cell’s height is that mode’s share within its own city, so every column fills the panel whatever its width. The consequence is the one a mosaic is drawn for: a cell’s area is the number of people in it, and a reader compares those areas across the whole panel without being asked to.

That is also what makes Millbrook readable rather than misleading. Its bicycle share is the largest of the four, and its column is the narrowest. So the plot reports the finding and the number of people it is based on at once, which four equal-width stacked bars cannot do.

The two axes therefore carry different quantities, so look at both before you read a value from either. The horizontal axis runs from 0 to the total in the data’s own units, 3,790 people. The vertical axis runs from 0 to 1 and can do nothing else, because what a height means is a share of its own column and the grand total is not the thing being divided.

Compose the partition with proportion and the horizontal axis reads shares of everyone surveyed instead:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(commutes) + zone * partition(city, mode, cross = TRUE) * proportion +
  x(people) + color(mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares")
(data(commutes) + zone * partition(col.city, col.mode, cross = True) * proportion +
  x(col.people) + color(col.mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares"))
data(commutes) +
  zone * partition(:city, :mode, cross = true) * proportion + x(:people) +
  color(:mode) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("Share of people surveyed") +
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares")
plot(data(commutes),
  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true }), proportion),
  x(col.people), color(col.mode),
  style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  x_label("Share of people surveyed"),
  title("The same mosaic, its width in shares"))

“Given the commutes: zones derived by partition through city and mode, crossed, and proportion, x is people, color by mode.”

The columns keep their widths, and the axis under them now runs from 0 to 1. Ashford’s column ends near 0.41, its share of the 3,790 people. The heights do not change, because each was already a share of its own column.

partition writes a name column holding each node’s own label, and a text layer reads it. The sunburst uses the same kind of layer. A shallower partition of the same table puts its nodes in exactly the same places, so the second layer needs no filtering and no arithmetic of its own.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(commutes) + x(people) +
  zone * partition(city, mode, cross = TRUE) + color(mode) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(city, cross = TRUE) + label(name) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The same plot, with its columns named")
(data(commutes) + x(col.people) +
  zone * partition(col.city, col.mode, cross = True) + color(col.mode) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(col.city, cross = True) + label(col.name) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The same plot, with its columns named"))
data(commutes) + x(:people) +
  zone * partition(:city, :mode, cross = true) + color(:mode) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(:city, cross = true) + label(:name) +
  x_label("People surveyed") +
  title("The same plot, with its columns named")
plot(data(commutes), x(col.people),
  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true })),
  color(col.mode), style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  layer(text, partition(col.city, { cross: true })), label(col.name),
  x_label("People surveyed"),
  title("The same plot, with its columns named"))

“Given the commutes: x is people, zones derived by partition through city and mode, crossed, colored by mode, and also text derived by partition through city, crossed, label by name.”

The labels are at the middle of each column because that is where the center of a column is, and style(nudge = ) is what moves them if you want them along the top. The city names would normally be on an axis. But gog’s category axis gives every slot the same width, and the mosaic’s columns all have different widths. So the names are drawn as a layer.

The cell edges are a style() setting like any other, and they matter more here than anywhere else in the book. Without them, two neighboring cells that share a color merge into one shape and the column boundary disappears:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(commutes) + zone * partition(city, mode, cross = TRUE) + x(people) +
  color(mode) + x_label("People surveyed") +
  title("The same plot with no edges")
(data(commutes) + zone * partition(col.city, col.mode, cross = True) + x(col.people) +
  color(col.mode) + x_label("People surveyed") +
  title("The same plot with no edges"))
data(commutes) + zone * partition(:city, :mode, cross = true) +
  x(:people) + color(:mode) + x_label("People surveyed") +
  title("The same plot with no edges")
plot(data(commutes),
  layer(zone, partition(col.city, col.mode, { cross: true })),
  x(col.people), color(col.mode), x_label("People surveyed"),
  title("The same plot with no edges"))

Both plots draw the same numbers. The second plot shows why a zone has the style(border_color = , border_size = ) settings at all. The mark has two uses. It is a highlight behind a line, where a frame would distract from the data, and it is the cells that are the data.

One level is legal and means something: the spine plot, columns of varying width and nothing dividing them, which is the marginal distribution on its own.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(commutes) + zone * partition(city, cross = TRUE) + x(people) +
  color(city) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The margin alone: a spine plot")
(data(commutes) + zone * partition(col.city, cross = True) + x(col.people) +
  color(col.city) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The margin alone: a spine plot"))
data(commutes) + zone * partition(:city, cross = true) + x(:people) +
  color(:city) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  x_label("People surveyed") + title("The margin alone: a spine plot")
plot(data(commutes), layer(zone, partition(col.city, { cross: true })),
  x(col.people), color(col.city),
  style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  x_label("People surveyed"), title("The margin alone: a spine plot"))

partition refuses the same things whether it is crossed or nested, because the refusals are about the tree and not about the layout. A level must be a categorical column, not a continuous one. A branch may stop early, but it may not skip a level and then continue. And an interior node carrying a value of its own is the one genuine ambiguity, so it is refused rather than guessed. The Polar chapter shows each refusal where it is easiest to see.

25.17 flow: a magnitude through its stages

Passengers are counted by class, then by whether they survived. The question is how many of each class reached each outcome.

flow is similar to partition in three ways. Both read categorical columns named in the atom, both place their own marks, and both supply more than one mark from one computation. Where partition divides a whole among nested parts, flow carries a magnitude through a sequence of stages. One row of the table is one path through every stage the atom names.

titanic: first 5 of 32 rows
class sex age survived n
1st Male Adult Yes 57
1st Male Adult No 118
1st Male Child Yes 5
1st Male Child No 0
1st Female Adult Yes 140
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + y(n) +
  ribbon * flow(class, survived) + color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) +
  title("Who survived, by class")
(data(titanic) + y(col.n) +
  ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  title("Who survived, by class"))
data(titanic) + y(:n) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) + color(:class) +
  zone * flow(:class, :survived) + title("Who survived, by class")
plot(data(titanic), y(col.n),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), color(col.class),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  title("Who survived, by class"))

“Given titanic: y is n, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, colored by class, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived.”

Three marks read a flow, and a full diagram layers all three:

Mark derived by flow Shape
ribbon * flow the bands between the stages, the plot above
zone * flow the slots at each stage
text * flow the name of each slot

The ribbon layer draws the bands, one per path, as thick as the path’s total at both ends. The zone layer draws each stage’s slots, stacked with no padding, so the measure axis is drawn with its usual ticks and reads true counts. A text layer names the slots. With shared = TRUE, two columns such as exporter and importer name one set of places, and every place lies on one axis, which carries no numbers. Drawn flat, it is the arc diagram; in polar(), it is the chord diagram. With layered = TRUE, each row is a link from one place to another, and gog computes a layer for each place from the links. That picture is the Sankey diagram. The Flow chapter builds the full diagram and gives the rules; this section only shows where the atom fits among the transforms.

25.18 layout: a graph placed from an edge table

partition, flow, layout and cluster each compute a whole picture rather than a column. layout is the third of them, and the first whose output draws in a space of its own. layout(from, to) reads the two endpoint columns of an edge table and computes a position for every distinct name, in the engine, the same way in every language. Three marks read the placement inside network(): edge the connections, point the nodes, text their names. Its positions mean nothing as quantities, so its space draws no axes. This section draws no layout plot. The Network chapter draws those plots and gives the rules; this section only shows where the atom fits among the transforms.

Mark derived by layout Shape
point * layout one dot per node
text * layout each node’s name
edge * layout one stroke per link

25.19 cluster: the closest leaves joined first

cluster is the fourth transform that computes a whole picture, and the question it answers is which things are most alike. It treats each category of an axis as a leaf of a tree, joins the two closest leaves, then the next two, and keeps joining until one tree holds them all. Each leaf is described by a profile: cluster(amount, over = nutrient) says that one leaf’s profile is its amount in every category of nutrient.

nutrients: first 5 of 40 rows
food nutrient amount
salmon protein 25.4
salmon fat 12.4
salmon carbs 0.0
salmon fiber 0.0
salmon iron 0.5
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(nutrients) + path * cluster(amount, over = nutrient) + x(food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")
(data(nutrients) + path * cluster(col.amount, over=col.nutrient) + x(col.food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))
data(nutrients) + path * cluster(:amount, over = :nutrient) + x(:food) +
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of")
plot(data(nutrients),
  layer(path, cluster(col.amount, { over: col.nutrient })), x(col.food),
  title("Eight foods, joined by what they are made of"))

“Given nutrients: paths derived by cluster on amount, over nutrient, x is food.”

Two marks read a cluster:

Mark derived by cluster Shape
zone * cluster the same leaves as cells, in the tree’s order
path * cluster the tree as joined strokes, the plot above

path draws the tree, and the height of a join says how different its two branches are. The same transform on zone reorders a tile plot’s slots to the tree’s leaf order. The Cluster chapter grows the tree, orders the tiles, and builds the clustered heatmap; this section only shows where the atom fits among the transforms.

25.20 dodge: side by side instead of on top

Every transform above answers a question about the data. The four that remain answer none. They change where a mark is drawn rather than what was measured. dodge is a different kind of transform: a collision modifier. It writes no new values; it moves marks that would otherwise be drawn at one position, and sets them side by side instead.

When color splits a bar, a box or an interval into groups, the groups share their category’s slot and are drawn on top of one another. A histogram reads well that way, because the overlapping bars are translucent. A grouped bar chart does not, because there you want the groups set side by side. dodge does exactly that:

gm_eras: first 5 of 284 rows
country continent year life population gdp era
Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530 1957
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803 2007
Albania Europe 1957 59.280 1476505 1942.2842 1957
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295 2007
Algeria Africa 1957 45.685 10270856 3013.9760 1957
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Mean life expectancy") +
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), y_label("Mean life expectancy"),
  title("Mean life expectancy by continent, 1957 vs 2007"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

Five marks take dodge. Three divide the slot’s width among their groups. A point moves sideways within the slot instead, and a text moves sideways to its own group’s bar:

Mark derived by dodge Shape
box * dodge one box per group, side by side in the slot
interval * dodge one whisker per group, side by side
point * dodge each point moved across the slot until none touch: the beeswarm
bar * dodge one bar per group, the plot above
text * dodge each group’s label over its own bar: Labels on dodged bars

The two eras are next to each other in every continent. Together they span the width one bar would. dodge divides that width into one part per group (G groups, each 1/G of it), and each bar leaves a fifth of its part empty, so the two do not touch. style(gap = ) sets that share; the space between continents does not change. And because the offset resolves the overlap outright, dodged bars take the same fill a single bar does. The translucent fill exists only to see through overlapping bars, and none overlap now.

It is written after * like any transform, so it composes cleanly: bar * mean * dodge aggregates first and dodges the result; box * dodge dodges a box’s own summary; interval * range * dodge dodges grouped whiskers. Here it sets each continent’s two distributions side by side:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy distribution, 1957 vs 2007")
(data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy distribution, 1957 vs 2007"))
data(gm_eras) + box * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Life expectancy distribution, 1957 vs 2007")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(box, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Life expectancy distribution, 1957 vs 2007"))

“Given the gapminder eras: boxes derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

Which marks dodge serves is decided by what a mark is. On bar, box and interval it subdivides a width (a bar’s thickness, a box’s body, a whisker’s slot). A point has no width, so dodge moves it instead. Each point moves sideways within its slot, only as far as it must to touch no other point, and never along the measure axis. A text has no width either, so dodge moves each label to its own group’s bar. An area is piled rather than subdivided (that is stack, the next section). Ask for dodge on an area and gog refuses, naming the collision modifier that fits. A line takes neither dodge nor stack. It is a thin stroke, so lines that meet cross rather than cover each other. The rest of the kernel follows the same rule: an atom combines with the marks it was defined for, and the refusal names the atom that fits rather than drawing something wrong.

On a bar, box, interval or text, dodge also needs a split to separate: a channel that splits the rows into groups, such as color or group. Without one there is a single mark per slot and nothing to set beside anything, so bar * dodge on its own is refused, and the message asks for the split. It is never accepted as a word that quietly does nothing. A point needs no split, because points in one slot can already land on one another. With a split, each group takes its own part of the slot, as a dodged bar does, and its points are moved apart inside that part:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + point * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  style(size = 2.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot")
(data(gm_eras) + point * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  style(size = 2.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot"))
data(gm_eras) + point * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) + color(:era) +
  style(size = 2.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(point, dodge), x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  color(col.era), style({ size: 2.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Each era swarms in its half of the slot"))

“Given the gapminder eras: points derived by dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era.”

The dots are drawn smaller here, with style(size = 2.5). Each era has half a slot, and at the default size Europe’s 2007 countries are too close together to fit in it, so gog would draw some of them at the edge and say how many.

25.21 stack: piled up, not side by side

Side by side, two eras’ populations never show what they add up to, and when the total means something the pile is the better picture.

stack is dodge’s sibling: the other way to resolve a color split’s overlap. Where dodge sets the groups beside each other, stack piles them on top of each other along the measure axis, each group starting where the one below it ended. It is the collision modifier for the marks that accumulate: bar and area pile heights, and point piles rows.

Take the dodge example, change dodge to stack, and sum population instead of averaging life expectancy:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.era) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * sum * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:era) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era), y_label("Population"),
  title("Population by continent, 1957 and 2007 stacked"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by sum and stack, x is continent, y is population, color by era.”

Three marks pile instead of overlapping:

Mark derived by stack Shape
area * stack each region starting at the top of the one below
point * bin * stack one dot per row, piled into a column, which is the dot plot
bar * stack one segment per group, piled, the plot above

The measure changed because you stack quantities that add up. Two populations can be added into one bar, while two mean life expectancies cannot: Europe’s two eras would pile into a bar reaching 144 years, so that comparison wants dodge, side by side. The grammar allows either, and the data decides which is right. Because the pile resolves the overlap, the bars take the same fill a single bar does, and the axis grows to the tallest stack: Asia passes five billion, the sum of its two eras.

Which marks stack serves is decided by what a mark is: the same rule dodge follows. What stack computes is one thing for every mark, a span from a foot to a top along the measure axis, and what differs is how a geometry draws that span. A bar fills it, and an area fills it across x. A point has no length to stretch across the span, so the span becomes how many dots there are, which is the dot plot. A box or interval is set beside its neighbors rather than piled, which is dodge. An unfilled line has nothing to fill and pile, so use area. A ribbon already spans a low to a high, so it measures no height from a baseline. Ask for stack on one of those and gog refuses, naming what fits instead. For bar and area it also needs a channel that splits the rows into groups to pile, such as color or group. bar * stack alone is refused, and the message asks for the split. It is never accepted as a word that quietly does nothing.

An estimated curve cannot be piled either. density computes each group’s curve at points along that group’s own range of values. The groups’ points do not line up, so stack has nothing to pile at one position:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + area * density * stack + x(life) + color(era)
data(gm_eras) + area * density * stack + x(col.life) + color(col.era)
data(gm_eras) + area * density * stack + x(:life) + color(:era)
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(area, density, stack), x(col.life),
  color(col.era))
Error:
! gog: `area * density * stack` piles the groups that land on one position, and `density` computes each group's curve at points along that group's own range, so the groups' points do not line up and nothing would pile. To compare the groups' curves, overlay them: `area * density + color(<group>) + style(opacity = 0.5)`, or give each group its own panel: `area * density | facet(<group>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To compare the shapes of the two eras, overlay them and make the fills partly transparent with style(opacity = 0.5), or give each era its own panel with | facet(era).

25.21.1 Stacked areas: the case stack was built for

A split area is where overlap matters most. Filled regions cover one another, and gog warns about it (the area chapter shows the warning and the opacity it suggests). Lowering the opacity does let you see through them, but five overlapping fills blend into colors the legend names for none of them. stack answers the same problem a different way. Each region starts at the cumulative height of the ones below, so they meet edge to edge in one band instead of covering each other, the classic “parts of a whole, over time”. The plot uses the gm_all table, shown in The same bin, cutting two axes:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(year) + y(population) + color(continent) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked")
(data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(col.year) + y(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked"))
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack + x(:year) + y(:population) +
  color(:continent) + y_label("Population") +
  title("World population by continent, stacked")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(area, sum, stack), x(col.year),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent), y_label("Population"),
  title("World population by continent, stacked"))

“Given all the gapminder years: areas derived by sum and stack, x is year, y is population, color by continent.”

Asia is at the bottom; Europe, Africa, the Americas and Oceania pile on top, and the band’s upper edge is the world total. It climbs from 2.4 billion people to 6.25 billion. Read any one color’s thickness for that continent’s population.

25.21.2 stack(share = TRUE): every pile filled to one

Reading a thickness is the hard part of the plot above, because each band’s baseline moves under it. When the composition is the question and the total is not, stack(share = TRUE) divides every pile by its own slot’s total, so all of them reach 1 and only the proportions are left. That is filling the pile:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(year) + y(population) +
  color(continent) + title("Every year's composition, filled to one")
(data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col.year) + y(col.population) +
  color(col.continent) + title("Every year's composition, filled to one"))
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:year) +
  y(:population) + color(:continent) +
  title("Every year's composition, filled to one")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(area, sum, stack({ share: true })), x(col.year),
  y(col.population), color(col.continent),
  title("Every year's composition, filled to one"))

“Given all the gapminder years: areas derived by sum and stack as shares, x is year, y is population, color by continent.”

Now Asia’s band holds about three fifths, and Europe’s visibly narrows across those 55 years. Both facts were also in the stacked plot before this one, where the rising total hid them. The axis says Share, because whatever the numbers were before, they are fractions of one now.

This is not a second name for proportion. The two divide by different totals. proportion divides by the whole plot’s, so its bars still say how big each slot is. This one divides by the slot’s own, which deliberately discards the slot’s size. So each year here is a set of shares of that year’s world population, a reading proportion cannot give in a single panel. Filling is a position adjustment: it changes where the marks are drawn and what the scale reads, never what was counted, which is why it belongs to stack and not to a statistic.

A bar fills the same way, and the result is the 100% stacked bar, worked through in the bar chapter. One parameter, both geometries, exactly as plain stack hands both marks the same span and lets each draw it: No Exceptions.

The axis of a filled pile runs from 0 to 1. As a percent, it runs from 0% to 100%, which is how a share is often read. Add percent = TRUE to y(). Here y() names population, the column sum adds up:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = TRUE) + x(year) +
  y(population, percent = TRUE) + color(continent)
(data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = True) + x(col.year) +
  y(col.population, percent = True) + color(col.continent))
data(gm_all) + area * sum * stack(share = true) + x(:year) +
  y(:population, percent = true) + color(:continent)
plot(data(gm_all), layer(area, sum, stack({ share: true })), x(col.year),
  y(col.population, { percent: true }), color(col.continent))

“Given all the gapminder years: areas derived by sum and stack as shares, x is year, y is population written as a percent, color by continent.”

Only the numbers on the axis change, as Scales explains.

25.21.3 stack(baseline = ): where the pile starts

Two things about a pile can be changed. Its heights are one, and share is how you change them. Where the pile starts is the other, and baseline is how you change that.

The default is "zero". Every pile starts at the axis, as in both plots above. That layout has a known weakness. Only the bottom band has a shape you can read. Every band above it rests on the sum of the bands below, so its shape carries all of their movement as well as its own.

The weakness is easiest to see when each series peaks at a different time. Here are four music genres over half a year, in the listening table:

listening: first 5 of 104 rows
week genre plays
1 Folk 38.0
2 Folk 36.4
3 Folk 38.6
4 Folk 39.5
5 Folk 38.3
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + area * stack + x(week) + y(plays) + color(genre) +
  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero")
(data(listening) + area * stack + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) + color(col.genre) +
  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero"))
data(listening) + area * stack + x(:week) + y(:plays) + color(:genre) +
  y_label("Plays") + title("Stacked on zero")
plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack), x(col.week), y(col.plays),
  color(col.genre), y_label("Plays"), title("Stacked on zero"))

Techno is the red band, the third from the bottom. It looks like it grows to about week 17 and then collapses. Part of that shape is Techno, and part of it is Folk and Jazz shrinking underneath it. You cannot tell which part is which.

"center" places each pile so that its middle is at zero:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver")
(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver"))
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "center") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("Centered: the ThemeRiver")
plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("Centered: the ThemeRiver"))

“Given the listening table: areas derived by stack on the center baseline, x is week, y is plays, color by genre.”

That symmetric layout is the ThemeRiver (Havre et al., 2000), named for the plot it was built to draw: how much each theme is written about, over time.

"wiggle" instead chooses the foot that leaves the bands as flat as possible. The thickest bands move least, because a reader looks at them first. The movement is pushed into the thin bands instead:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph")
(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph"))
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("Flattest: the streamgraph")
plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "wiggle" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("Flattest: the streamgraph"))

“Given the listening table: areas derived by stack on the wiggle baseline, x is week, y is plays, color by genre.”

Now Techno is one clean shape, widening and then narrowing, which is what the numbers actually say. Folk, the blue band, is a steady decline rather than a wedge. No band changed thickness between these three plots. Only the starting place of each pile changed.

The last plot is a streamgraph (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008). The middle one is a ThemeRiver. The two are often confused and they are not the same layout: one is symmetric, the other is chosen to reduce movement. The streamgraph’s designers argue readers compare values more accurately on it, and that argument is the reason this option exists (Byron & Wattenberg, 2008).

Notice also that these two plots have no numbers on the measure axis. Once a pile has moved off zero, no value on that axis means anything. A band drawn from 12 to 20 says “this group is 8 here”, and the 12 and the 20 only record where the pile was placed. So gog draws no ticks and no axis label of its own, for the same reason it leaves an empty heatmap cell unpainted. A label you write with y_label() is still drawn, because it names the quantity and not a position. The scale is unchanged, so thicknesses stay comparable everywhere in the plot, and thickness is what a streamgraph asks you to read.

baseline is not an area-only parameter. A bar has a pile too, so it is placed the same way:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars")
(data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars"))
data(listening) + bar * stack(baseline = "center") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + title("The same baseline, drawn as bars")
plot(data(listening), layer(bar, stack({ baseline: "center" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre),
  title("The same baseline, drawn as bars"))

One parameter, both geometries. share follows the same rule, and so does plain stack, which hands both marks one span and lets each draw it: No Exceptions.

Once a pile is moved, zero on the measure axis no longer means anything. Only a flat plot can work without a meaningful zero, so the other spaces refuse:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(week) + y(plays) +
  color(genre) + polar()
(data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) +
  color(col.genre) + polar())
data(listening) + area * stack(baseline = "wiggle") + x(:week) +
  y(:plays) + color(:genre) + polar()
plot(data(listening), layer(area, stack({ baseline: "wiggle" })),
  x(col.week), y(col.plays), color(col.genre), polar())
Error:
! gog: `stack(baseline = "wiggle")` moves every pile off the origin of the measure axis, and `polar()` has no origin to spare. A displaced pile is a statement about a plane: in `polar()` the measure is an angle or a radius or a height the space has already fixed, so moving the foot asks for a place that is not on the plot. Keep the space and drop the baseline (`stack` alone, or with its `share` set to true for composition), or keep the baseline and draw it flat.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

In polar() the measure is an angle or a radius. A radius of zero is the center of the circle, so moving a pile off it asks for a negative radius, which is not a place on the plot.

25.21.4 A pile has one direction

stack has a third condition. The first two, a mark that can pile and a channel that splits the rows, are about the sentence. This one is about the numbers.

In a table of sales and returns, the returns arrive as negative numbers. The question is then whether a pile can grow downward at all.

A pile puts its groups end to end. Every member must therefore point the same way.

Negative values are allowed. A pile of them grows downward from zero, exactly as a positive pile grows up:

drawdown: first 5 of 6 rows
quarter cost kind
Q1 -5 refunds
Q2 -4 refunds
Q3 -6 refunds
Q1 -3 chargebacks
Q2 -2 chargebacks
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(drawdown) + bar * stack + x(quarter) + y(cost) + color(kind) +
  y_label("Cost") + title("A pile that grows down")
(data(drawdown) + bar * stack + x(col.quarter) + y(col.cost) + color(col.kind) +
  y_label("Cost") + title("A pile that grows down"))
data(drawdown) + bar * stack + x(:quarter) + y(:cost) + color(:kind) +
  y_label("Cost") + title("A pile that grows down")
plot(data(drawdown), layer(bar, stack), x(col.quarter), y(col.cost),
  color(col.kind), y_label("Cost"), title("A pile that grows down"))

A pile whose values point in two directions has no correct drawing. Suppose one group is 5 and another is -3 at the same position. The negative band would begin where the first band ended, at 5, and reach back down to 2. That region already belongs to the first group. A reader would see a solid block of length 3 where the number is negative. So gog refuses:

mixed_signs: first 5 of 6 rows
quarter amount kind
Q1 5 sales
Q2 5 sales
Q3 5 sales
Q1 2 returns
Q2 -3 returns
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(mixed_signs) + bar * stack + x(quarter) + y(amount) + color(kind)
data(mixed_signs) + bar * stack + x(col.quarter) + y(col.amount) + color(col.kind)
data(mixed_signs) + bar * stack + x(:quarter) + y(:amount) + color(:kind)
plot(data(mixed_signs), layer(bar, stack), x(col.quarter), y(col.amount),
  color(col.kind))
Error:
! gog: `bar * stack` piles the groups at one position on top of one another, and at quarter = Q2 they disagree in sign — `sales` is 5 and `returns` is -3. A pile has one direction: the band going the other way is drawn *inside* the ones below it, so the plot would show a block of 3 where the number is negative and read its sign backwards. Either keep the sign and drop the pile — `bar * dodge` sets the groups side by side instead, and a dodged bar keeps its own baseline, so a negative one hangs below the axis where a reader can see that it is negative — or keep the pile and drop the sign, stacking magnitudes you took the absolute value of in the host. (A pile whose members agree stays legal both ways: all-negative grows downward from zero exactly as all-positive grows up.)
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names the position, both groups, and both numbers. A message that said only “some values are negative” would make you search the whole table for a pile you cannot see on the page.

There are two ways to fix this, and you choose by what you want the plot to show. If the sign matters, use dodge. Each bar then keeps its own baseline, so a negative bar hangs below the axis where a reader can see that it is negative. If the total matters, take the absolute value in the host language first. You are then stacking magnitudes, so say so in the column name or the axis label.

stack(share = TRUE) fails for the same reason, and the failure is easier to see. A share is a fraction of the pile’s total. Here the total is 5 plus -3, which is 2, so the two shares are 2.5 and -1.5. No rescaling fixes that. The problem is in the pile itself, not in how the pile is drawn.

Piles at different positions may still point different ways. Each pile is read on its own. One quarter can be positive and the next negative in the same plot.

25.21.5 A pile holds one value for each group

stack has a fourth condition. Like the third, it is about the table rather than the sentence. At each position, a pile holds one value for each group. The gm_eras table has one row for each country in each era, so Africa has 52 rows for 1957 and 52 for 2007. stack piles the groups, not the rows inside one group. All the rows of one era would start at the same height and cover one another, so gog refuses:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era)
data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.era)
data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) + color(:era)
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era))
Error:
! gog: `bar * stack` piles one value for each group at a position, and at `continent = Africa` 52 rows have `era = 1957` (10 of the 10 position and group pairs hold more than one row). Those rows would all start from the same foot and cover one another, while the groups above would be lifted by all of them, so the pile would show none of its rows. To draw one segment for each group, summarize the rows first: `bar * sum * stack` adds them, and `mean`, `median`, `max` and `min` work the same way. To draw one segment for each row, split by a column that names each row as well: `+ group(country)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names the first pile with repeated rows. It says that all ten continent and era pairs have them, and it offers two fixes. Which fix you choose depends on what each segment should show. To draw one segment for each era, summarize the rows first. That is the first plot of stack, with sum before stack. To draw one segment for each row, add a second split, by a column whose value differs in every row of a pile. Here that column is country, in the gm_eras table, shown in dodge: side by side instead of on top:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(continent) + y(population) + color(era) +
  group(country) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Every country in each era, its own segment")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) + color(col.era) +
  group(col.country) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Every country in each era, its own segment"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * stack + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  color(:era) + group(:country) + y_label("Population") +
  title("Every country in each era, its own segment")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), color(col.era), group(col.country),
  y_label("Population"),
  title("Every country in each era, its own segment"))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by stack, x is continent, y is population, color by era, grouped by country.”

Every country in each era is now one thin segment, and each pile reaches the same total as with sum.

25.21.6 The dot plot

A histogram’s bars hide the rows inside them. When every country should stay visible, and countable, the mark to pile is the point.

A point has no length, so it cannot stretch across the span every other mark gets. gog fills the span with copies of the point instead: one dot per unit, piled up from the foot. The unit of a count is one row, so a pile of dots is a count you can count. The dots are the countries of the gapminder_2007 table, shown in the bin section:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, bin, stack), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"), title("One dot per country"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by bin and stack, x is life.”

That is a dot plot (Wilkinson, 1999), and it is the same sentence as the histogram at the top of this chapter with one atom changed and one added. Compare the two. bar * bin draws each tally as a length, and you read the shape from the outline. point * bin * stack draws each tally as that many dots, so every country in the table is on the page. Count the tallest pile and you get its bin’s count exactly, which no bar can offer.

Nothing here is a color split, and none is needed. bar and area pile groups, so they ask for one; a point piles rows, which every table already has. What it asks for instead is a transform that counts them, because a pile of 3.7 dots means nothing:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * mean * stack + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, mean, stack), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `point * stack` piles one dot per observation along the measure axis — the dot plot — so the measure has to be a count of rows, and nothing here counts them. Add the transform that does: `point * bin * stack` for a continuous axis (dots per interval), `point * count * stack` for a categorical one (dots per category).
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The refusal names the two transforms that count rows: bin for a continuous axis, and count for a categorical one. The second draws a bar chart of counts as piles of dots, one dot per row:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(col.continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + x(:continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count, stack), x(col.continent),
  title("One dot per country, piled by continent"))

The dots pack tightly here and loosely on a small table. No setting controls the spacing. The vertical gap between stacked dots is always one count unit on the y axis, so its size on the page depends on the tallest pile. A taller pile therefore subdivides the panel more finely, and a pile of ten dots in a tall panel leaves wide gaps. style(size = ) will enlarge the dots, but making them touch means fixing the panel’s height to the tallest pile, and no setting does that. The y axis shows real counts either way, and that choice is deliberate: the alternative is to draw the dots touching and leave the axis with no meaning.

Each pile’s height is the count, drawn on y, so this dot plot names no column there. Name continent on both x and y, and gog refuses it. The message suggests color(continent) or a facet instead.

Writing bin is not enough when a summary follows it. bin hands its measure job to the summary, such as mean, so the pile would again be a number rather than a count of rows, and gog refuses it in the same way. A running count is refused too, because cumulative counts every earlier row again in each later bin, and a dot would then stand for one row many times:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * mean * stack + x(life) + y(gdp)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * mean * stack + x(col.life) + y(col.gdp)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * mean * stack + x(:life) + y(:gdp)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, bin, mean, stack), x(col.life),
  y(col.gdp))
Error:
! gog: `point * bin * mean * stack` piles one dot per observation, the dot plot, so the measure has to be a count of rows, and here `mean` measures each bin instead of counting its rows. A pile of that number is not a count of anything. Keep whichever you meant: `point * bin * stack` to pile the rows of each bin, or `point * bin * mean` for one point at each bin's value.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

color() is how a dot plot splits its rows by a category. On the dot plot of life expectancy, each dot takes the color of its row’s continent, and each pile keeps its height:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(life) + color(continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country, colored by continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(col.life) + color(col.continent) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("One dot per country, colored by continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * bin * stack + x(:life) +
  color(:continent) + x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("One dot per country, colored by continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, bin, stack), x(col.life),
  color(col.continent), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("One dot per country, colored by continent"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by bin and stack, x is life, color by continent.”

The four piles left of 60 years hold 39 dots, and 38 of them are African. The last pile holds 32 dots, and 18 of them are European.

The piles of the continent dot plot can also be horizontal, as bars can. Write y(continent) in place of x(continent). The count is then drawn along x, and each pile grows to the right:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + y(continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled to the right by continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + y(col.continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled to the right by continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count * stack + y(:continent) +
  title("One dot per country, piled to the right by continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count, stack), y(col.continent),
  title("One dot per country, piled to the right by continent"))

25.21.7 How many rows is too many?

One dot per country works at 142 rows. A table twelve times that size is where the picture stops working.

Write the same sentence for a much larger table and the dots in each pile merge into one solid shape. The gm_all table, shown in The same bin, cutting two axes, holds every year of gapminder rather than one. That is 1704 rows, and the tallest pile is 314 of them:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots")
(data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(col.life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots"))
data(gm_all) + point * bin * stack + x(:life) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin, stack), x(col.life),
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("Every year, every country: 1704 dots"))
gog: `point * bin * stack` piled 314 dots into one column, and at that height they overlap instead of counting — a dot plot says what it says by showing every observation separately, so this is a histogram drawn dot by dot. For this many rows, `bar * bin` reads the same shape as a summary, and `line * density` as a curve. `style(size = )` shrinks the dots, which buys a little room.

gog draws it, and says what happened. The piles have become solid sticks. With 314 dots in a pile, the gap is a sixth of a dot’s width, so the dots overlap and nothing can be counted, which was this plot’s entire claim. What you are looking at is a histogram drawn dot by dot, and a costly one: it draws 1704 circles where bar * bin draws twelve rectangles.

The warning is not a row limit, and that matters. It compares the gap against one dot’s diameter, both of which gog knows once the panel is laid out. So the warning appears exactly when the picture degrades, and not when it does not. With wider bins, a smaller table gets the warning too. Shrink the dots with style(size = ) far enough and the warning stops. On this table, though, that means style(size = 0.75), a dot 1.5 pixels wide and too small to count, because size is the dot’s radius. That is why the next plot also cuts more bins. A number like “more than 500 rows” would be wrong at some panel size or dot size, and there is no need to guess one when the real condition is available.

Which also means the warning is advice, not a limit. Two atoms usually answer it without removing a single dot, and the first is the one people forget: more bins spread the same rows over more piles, so every pile gets shorter without anything getting smaller. Then the dots themselves:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller")
