(data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(col.life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") + title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller"))
data(gm_all) + point * bin(40) * stack + x(:life) + style(size = 1.5) +
  x_label("Life expectancy (years)") +
  title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller")
plot(data(gm_all), layer(point, bin(40), stack), x(col.life),
  style({ size: 1.5 }), x_label("Life expectancy (years)"),
  title("The same 1704 rows, cut finer and drawn smaller"))

“Given all the gapminder years: points derived by bin into 40 and stack, x is life, with size 1.5.”

The columns are made of visible dots again, and every one of the 1704 is still on the page. Faceting is the third way, since fewer rows per panel means shorter piles in each.

What none of them changes is the arithmetic. Counting needs at least one dot-diameter of axis per row, so the tallest pile you can still count is about the panel’s height divided by a dot. That is a few hundred with dots you can see, and a few dozen if you mean to count them one by one. Past that, a summary is the better answer, and the reason is the same one that makes the dot plot useful for small tables. A bin width or a bandwidth is a guess about structure when there are thirty rows. It is a reliable description when there are ten thousand. So the dot plot stops working at the same size where a summary starts working well.

25.21.8 One bar, split into its parts

Not every question has a category for the x axis. Here the rows are the 264 wind observations of the winds table, shown in The same count, tallying two axes. Together they make one total, and the only question is how that total divides by direction.

Every stacked bar so far has been drawn at a position, one pile per category on the x axis. Take the position away and the split still has something to divide: a single bar, showing how one total divides.

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(direction)
data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(col.direction)
data(winds) + bar * count * stack + color(:direction)
plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count, stack), color(col.direction))

“Given the winds: bars derived by count and stack, color by direction.”

There is no x() in that sentence, and none is needed. A bar normally requires a position because it has to be drawn somewhere. Here the color split is what divides the bar into parts, and there is one slot for those parts to share, so the position is no longer required. Bend this same plot into a circle and it is a pie, the subject of Polar.

Without a split there is nothing to divide, so the position is required again and the refusal says so. The statistic also has to be one that means something with nothing to group by. count and sum reduce a set of rows to one number. bin and density describe how values spread along an axis, and there is no axis here.

A single bar can also be horizontal when it adds up a column. With sum, the bar is drawn along the axis where you name that column. Here x(population) gives the bar’s length, not a position:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * stack + x(population) + color(continent) +
  title("The world's population, divided by continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * stack + x(col.population) + color(col.continent) +
  title("The world's population, divided by continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum * stack + x(:population) +
  color(:continent) +
  title("The world's population, divided by continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.population),
  color(col.continent),
  title("The world's population, divided by continent"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum and stack, x is population, color by continent.”

The bar’s length is the world’s population in 2007, about 6.25 billion people. Asia’s part is about three fifths of it.

That ends the sections on stack. Two collision modifiers remain: jitter, which spreads points within a category, and repel, which moves labels apart.

25.22 jitter: spread sideways, along the category

dodge and stack resolve the overlap of grouped marks. The third collision modifier resolves a mark’s own points landing on top of each other, as dodge also does on a point. jitter does it another way: it moves each point sideways by a small amount that varies from point to point. A strip plot, every country as a dot above its continent, draws its points in a single vertical line, and heavy overlap hides how many there are:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.life),
  style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Strip plot: the points pile onto one line"))

jitter nudges each point a little to the side, so the crowded points spread out and the shape of each group shows:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(continent) + y(life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + style(opacity = 0.5) +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("point * jitter: the same points, spread to show density"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter, x is continent, y is life.”

Africa’s long tail of low values and Europe’s tight cluster near the top were both there before; the spread is what lets you read them.

jitter moves a point along the categorical axis, never along the measured one. Look again: every dot is at exactly the same height as before; the spread is entirely sideways. This is the rule, not a coincidence. The horizontal axis is a category, and a category has no magnitude, so nudging a point along it changes nothing you could misread. The vertical axis is a measurement, and moving a point off its measured value would misreport the data, so jitter never touches it. (Spreading in both directions is the other way to do this. It moves a point off its measured value, which is why gog spreads along one axis only.) On a horizontal strip, with the category on y, the spread is vertical instead. jitter always spreads the categorical axis and leaves the measured one exact.

The spread is deterministic: it is computed from the data itself, not from a random-number generator or the clock, so the same plot drawn twice is pixel-for-pixel the same picture. A specification always means one plot.

25.22.1 How much to spread: jitter(amount)

The default spread is one guess at what reads well, and on your figure it may be too wide or too narrow.

By default a point moves at most 0.4 of a slot from its category’s center: far enough to show how many points there are, and near enough to leave a gap between categories. For a wider or narrower spread, jitter(amount) multiplies the default by a plain number, so jitter(0.5) is half as wide (a bare jitter is jitter(1)).

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(continent) + y(life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(0.5) + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  style(opacity = 0.5) + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter(0.5)), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), style({ opacity: 0.5 }), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("point * jitter(0.5): a tighter spread"))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by jitter at 0.5, x is continent, y is life.”

The amount can be any number from 0 to 1.25. jitter(0) moves no point. It is harmless, so gog draws the plot and prints a note that the jitter did nothing. At the other end, jitter(1.25) moves a point up to half a slot, to the edge of its slot. gog refuses a larger amount, because it would move some points into a neighboring category, where they would be read as that category’s rows:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(continent) + y(life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(col.continent) + y(col.life)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * jitter(2) + x(:continent) + y(:life)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, jitter(2)), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life))
Error:
! gog: `jitter(2)` spreads points past the edge of their own category, so some would land in the neighboring one and be read as its rows. A point moves up to 0.4 of a slot for each unit of the amount, so `jitter(1.25)` reaches the slot's edge and is the widest spread that keeps every point in its own category. Use an amount of 1.25 or less; to show where many points overlap, `style(opacity = )` or a smaller `style(size = )` does it without moving any point.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message names 1.25 as the widest amount, and style(opacity = ) as a way to show where points overlap without moving any of them.

The parameter has the same shape as density’s adjust, a dimensionless multiple of an automatic value. It is there for the same reason density and bin take a parameter while dodge does not. The jitter amount is a legibility choice with no single right value, whereas gog computes dodge’s offsets itself: from the group count on a bar, and from the other points in the slot on a point. A value you must choose takes a parameter; a value gog can compute does not.

Like dodge on a point, jitter needs no color split. It separates a mark’s own points where they land on one another, so point * jitter with only x and y is a whole sentence. It also needs a categorical position axis to spread within. Ask for jitter when both x and y are continuous and gog refuses. There is no slot to spread across, and no axis it could move a point along without misplacing its value. The answer for overplotting on two continuous axes is style(opacity = ), which shows where points are crowded without moving any of them.

Which marks jitter serves is decided by what a mark is: the rule that divides the whole trio. jitter spreads a scatter of individual points, so it is defined for point alone. A bar, box or interval has a width, and its groups are set apart by dodge; a line or area is one connected shape, not scattered points. Ask for jitter on any of those and gog refuses, naming the collision modifier that fits.

Three of the four collision modifiers divide the marks by geometry and by axis: dodge sets marks side by side within a slot, stack accumulates along the measure axis, jitter spreads along the categorical one. Each mark that dodge, stack or jitter serves has an answer to overlap that moves nothing off its value, and point has three. It is the one mark that can collide on either axis. Along a measure, it is piled into a countable stack of dots. Along a category, it is moved sideways within its slot, by jitter or by dodge. All three are modifiers the kernel already has, so these uses of point need no new atom.

25.23 repel: move the labels off each other

The fourth collision modifier answers a collision the first three cannot see. They all resolve marks that landed on one position, which is a fact about the data. A label is as wide as the word it draws, so two labels overlap at positions their points never shared, and no modifier computed from a position can find them. Thirty European countries, each named:

gm_europe: first 5 of 30 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.030
Austria Europe 2007 79.829 8199783 36126.493
Belgium Europe 2007 79.441 10392226 33692.605
Bosnia and Herzegovina Europe 2007 74.852 4552198 7446.299
Bulgaria Europe 2007 73.005 7322858 10680.793
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The names overlap")
(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The names overlap"))
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text + x(:gdp) +
  y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The names overlap")
plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("The names overlap"))

text * repel measures the space each label will take, and moves the labels until no two words overlap:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("text * repel: the same names, moved apart")
(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("text * repel: the same names, moved apart"))
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("text * repel: the same names, moved apart")
plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("text * repel: the same names, moved apart"))

“Given gapminder Europe: points, and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”

No two names overlap now. A label that ends up more than a line of text away from its point is joined to it by a thin line. Two rules set where each label rests. First, a label rests beside its dot, on whichever side has room. repel pulls the label toward its dot and pushes it away from every word and every dot, and the label stops where the two balance. A label with no neighbors is just above its dot. One with neighbors moves to whichever side is free. Second, when a label is pushed by another label and by its own dot at the same time, it moves off the other label and may rest over its dot. A word over a dot is still readable. Two words over each other are not.

Like jitter, the placement is deterministic: it depends only on the labels and the rows, never on a random-number generator, so one specification always draws the same picture. Like jitter, it needs no color split, since what it separates is the layer’s own labels.

repel takes no parameter, and jitter takes one, for the same reason. A jitter’s spread has no single right value, so you choose it. A label moves exactly as far as the overlap requires and no further. That distance is computed, the way dodge computes a width, so there is nothing to set. The gap left between two labels is set by the font size. The engine sets the distance of style(nudge = ) from the font size in the same way.

Above some number of labels, no placement fits at all. repel draws every one of them anyway and reports how many still overlap. A plot missing the names it could not fit would read as a plot with fewer rows, and nobody looking at it would know.

repel is text-only. Each of the other three serves the marks whose geometry fits it, and a label is the only glyph made of a word. Ask for it on a point and gog refuses, naming jitter; on a bar it names dodge. Its counterpart among the settings is style(nudge = ), a fixed shift in a direction you name, described in Text. The two compose: the nudge says which side a label prefers, and repel resolves the overlaps that remain.

The four collision modifiers are one family, and two questions divide it. Three of them ask what geometry does this mark have, and answer with a width, a measure or a slot. The fourth asks what is this mark made of, and only one mark is made of words.

25.24 cumulative: the running total

How much has been sold so far this year? In which week did one genre’s plays pass another’s? A running total answers both: each value is added to the values before it, so each position shows the total so far. stack adds up the groups that share one position, and cumulative adds up the positions of one group. sum adds the rows of a category into one number, while cumulative keeps every position. It follows the order of the axis: from the smallest value to the largest on a continuous axis, and in the categories’ own order on a category axis.

The actuals table holds the sales of one year in each row:

actuals: all 5 rows
year sales
2019 120
2020 135
2021 128
2022 152
2023 168
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(actuals) + line * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) +
  title("Sales so far")
(data(actuals) + line * cumulative + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) +
  title("Sales so far"))
data(actuals) + line * cumulative + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  title("Sales so far")
plot(data(actuals), layer(line, cumulative), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  title("Sales so far"))

“Given the actuals: a line derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales.”

The line starts at 120, the sales of 2019, and ends at 703, the sales of all five years together. y(sales) names the column that is added up. The axis is labeled “Cumulative”, because it shows the total, not the sales of one year.

cumulative measures nothing itself. It adds up what the layer measures: the column named on y, as here, or the measurement that a transform before it writes. The marks that draw one value at each position draw the total. A bar or an area grows from zero, a line, a step or a point is drawn at the total, and text prints it. The other marks refuse cumulative. With several rows at one position, write sum first, as in line * sum * cumulative, so that each position adds one number.

When color splits the rows, each group adds up its own total, as each group gets its own statistic. The listening table, shown in the section on stack(baseline = ), holds the weekly plays of four music genres:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(listening) + line * cumulative + x(week) + y(plays) + color(genre) +
  title("Plays so far, by genre")
(data(listening) + line * cumulative + x(col.week) + y(col.plays) + color(col.genre) +
  title("Plays so far, by genre"))
data(listening) + line * cumulative + x(:week) + y(:plays) +
  color(:genre) + title("Plays so far, by genre")
plot(data(listening), layer(line, cumulative), x(col.week), y(col.plays),
  color(col.genre), title("Plays so far, by genre"))

“Given the listening table: lines derived by cumulative, x is week, y is plays, color by genre.”

Folk has the most plays for the first 19 weeks. Techno has few plays in the first weeks, and it passes Folk in week 20. After 26 weeks, Techno has 674 plays in total and Folk has 515. Each line adds up the weeks of its own genre.

25.24.1 A running count

After count or bin, the measurement is a number of rows, so the total is a running count. Here each bar is the number of countries in its continent and in every continent before it on the axis. A label prints each continent’s own count:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(continent) +
  text * count * cumulative + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Running count of countries, by continent")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(col.continent) +
  text * count * cumulative + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Running count of countries, by continent"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(:continent) +
  text * count * cumulative + label(:count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Running count of countries, by continent")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count, cumulative),
  x(col.continent), layer(text, count, cumulative), label(col.count),
  style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Running count of countries, by continent"))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count and cumulative, x is continent, and also text derived by count and cumulative, label by count, with nudge up.”

The last bar is 142, every country in the table. Africa’s bar is 52 countries taller than Europe’s, and 52 is the number on Africa’s label. The total is written to a column named cumulative, while count keeps each continent’s own count. So label(count) prints the count of each continent, and label(cumulative) would print the total so far.

On a continuous axis, bin cuts the axis into bins first. A step through the running counts is the cumulative frequency curve, also called an ogive:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + step * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
  title("Countries up to each life expectancy")
(data(gapminder_2007) + step * bin * cumulative + x(col.life) +
  title("Countries up to each life expectancy"))
data(gapminder_2007) + step * bin * cumulative + x(:life) +
  title("Countries up to each life expectancy")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(step, bin, cumulative), x(col.life),
  title("Countries up to each life expectancy"))

“Given gapminder 2007: a step outline derived by bin and cumulative, x is life.”

Each flat part is at the number of countries whose life expectancy is in that bin or a lower one. The curve rises most over its last three bins, from about 68 to 83 years. Those three bins hold 84 of the 142 countries.

25.24.2 Ending at 1: cumulative(share = TRUE)

cumulative(share = TRUE) divides each total by the last total of its group, so every group ends at 1. Each line then shows the share of a group’s rows up to each value: the group’s empirical CDF. On a continuous axis, count tallies the rows at each distinct value, so the line rises at every value that occurs. The plot uses the iris_flowers table, shown in the range section:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(iris_flowers) + step * count * cumulative(share = TRUE) + x(petal_length) +
  color(species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Share of each species, by petal length")
(data(iris_flowers) + step * count * cumulative(share = True) + x(col.petal_length) +
  color(col.species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Share of each species, by petal length"))
data(iris_flowers) + step * count * cumulative(share = true) +
  x(:petal_length) + color(:species) + x_label("Petal length (cm)") +
  title("Share of each species, by petal length")
plot(data(iris_flowers), layer(step, count, cumulative({ share: true })),
  x(col.petal_length), color(col.species), x_label("Petal length (cm)"),
  title("Share of each species, by petal length"))

“Given the iris flowers: step outlines derived by count and cumulative as shares, x is petal length, color by species.”

Each line reaches 1 at the longest petal of its species: 1.9 cm for setosa, 5.1 cm for versicolor and 6.9 cm for virginica. After that, the line stays at 1, and before the shortest petal of its species it is at 0. A running total has a value at every position on the axis, for every group. Where a group has no rows, its total is the total so far, or 0 before its first row. That is also why stacked running totals stay correct: each group starts at the totals below it, even where a group below has no rows. Each passes one half at the 25th of its 50 petals: 1.5 cm, 4.3 cm and 5.5 cm. Setosa’s line has 9 flat parts, one for each petal length that occurs in that species. With bin in place of count, the line has one flat part for each bin instead.

proportion cannot draw this plot. It divides by the total of the whole plot, so each species’ line would end at one third, its share of all 150 flowers. gog refuses proportion beside cumulative, and the message points to share.

25.24.3 The order of a category axis

On a category axis, the total is added up in the order of the categories. That is the order your table declares, or else the order in which the categories first appear in its rows. gog adds up the totals in that order, and places the categories on the axis after that. With order(count, desc = TRUE), Africa would move to the first slot and keep its total of 115, so the bars would no longer rise from left to right. That sentence is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(continent) +
  order(count, desc = TRUE)
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(col.continent) +
  order(col.count, desc = True))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count * cumulative + x(:continent) +
  order(:count, desc = true)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count, cumulative),
  x(col.continent), order(col.count, { desc: true }))
Error:
! gog: `order(count)` would sort the categories of `continent` after `bar * count * cumulative` has added them up in their own order, so each total would stand at a category it was not added at. gog does not add up in a sorted order yet. Declare the order in the table instead (a factor in R, `ordered()` in Python, Julia and JavaScript), and the totals are added up in that order.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To choose the order, declare it in the table: as a factor in R, or with ordered() in Python, Julia and JavaScript. The totals are then added up in that order. A facet or play splits the rows before any transform runs, so each panel or frame adds up its own rows.

cumulative does not draw a waterfall chart. Each block of a waterfall is one change, and it starts at the total before it, so its length is the change and not the total. Zone draws one from columns that your table computes.

25.25 Columns a transform writes

Many sentences in this book name a column that their table does not have. A histogram binds y(count), a flow diagram binds label(name), and a network binds size(degree). None of those tables has a count, a name or a degree column. In each case, the transform writes that column. A transform runs before anything is drawn, and it can write columns that your table never held. A sentence names some of those columns the way it names any other column. The transform sets each name, and a sentence must use it exactly.

25.25.1 The name on a measure axis

When they read one column, bin, count, proportion and density write their measurement on y, and they name it themselves. bin and count name it count, proportion names it proportion, and density names it density. When proportion follows bin or count, as in bar * bin * proportion, the bars are shares, so the name is proportion. When cumulative follows them, as in step * bin * cumulative, the axis holds running totals, so the name is cumulative. You can write that name in y(), or leave y() out. Either way, the axis is labeled with that name, capitalized: “Count”, “Proportion”, “Density” or “Cumulative”. Write the name, such as y(count), when the axis needs a setting such as limits.

Any other name in y() is refused. In other sentences, a name in y() chooses the column to draw. Here the transform has already chosen it, so a new name would change only the label on the axis. gog refuses it and points to y_label(), which sets the axis label:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y(countries)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + y(col.countries)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + y(:countries)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  y(col.countries))
Error:
! gog: `bar * count` draws counts on `y`, in a column it names `count`, so `y()` takes that name or none. `countries` is not a column of the table, so `y(countries)` would change only the axis label. Write `y(count)`, which still takes the axis's settings such as `limits`, or leave `y()` out. To choose the label, write `y_label("Countries")`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

y_label() changes the label and nothing else:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + y_label("Countries") +
  title("The label comes from y_label()")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + y_label("Countries") +
  title("The label comes from y_label()"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  y_label("Countries") + title("The label comes from y_label()")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  y_label("Countries"), title("The label comes from y_label()"))

The bars are the same counts. Only the axis label changes, to Countries.

Because a new name is refused, a misspelled one is refused too. y(cuont) would otherwise draw an axis labeled “Cuont”, and gog says it looks like count. Two other kinds of name are refused for the same reason. The first is a column of your table: bar * bin + x(life) + y(gdp) would label counts as gdp. The second is the name of another transform. On a histogram, y(density) would label counts as a density, so gog refuses it and names the transform that computes one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) + y(density)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) + y(col.density)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + y(:density)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life), y(col.density))
Error:
! gog: `bar * bin` draws counts on `y`, in a column it names `count`, so `y()` takes that name or none. `density` is the name of a transform, so `y(density)` would label the axis `density` over counts. For a density curve, `line * density + x(life)` estimates one. Write `y(count)`, which still takes the axis's settings such as `limits`, or leave `y()` out. To choose a different label, write `y_label()`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message offers line * density for a density curve. To keep the bars and change their heights, write bar * bin * proportion: each bar is then its bin’s share of all the rows. A share is not a density, but a density histogram on the same bins has the same shape. To show a density curve and a histogram together, put them in two plots, one above the other, as One variable shows. In one panel the pair is refused.

A stack that fills each pile to one, stack(share = TRUE), keeps the transform’s name, such as count for bin, because it rescales the values in their own column. Its axis is labeled “Share” even when you write y(count). Horizontal bars follow the same rule, with x() and x_label().

25.25.2 Other columns a transform writes

When bin, count, proportion and density read two columns, one on each position, they write their measurement to color rather than to an axis. partition, flow, layout and cluster also write columns with names of their own, and a sentence must use each name exactly. For each column, the table lists what it holds, how a sentence names it, and where it is drawn:

Column Written by What it holds Named with Drawn in
count zone * bin, zone * count the number of rows in each cell color(count) Zone
proportion zone * proportion each cell’s share of all the rows color(proportion) Zone
density zone * density, surface * density the estimate in each cell or face color(density) Zone, Surface
level path * density the value each contour ring was traced at color(level) Path
name partition, flow, layout the name of each node or slot label(name), which a text layer derived by these transforms may leave out, and under flow also brush(name) Polar, Flow, Network
depth partition the ring a node is on, counting the innermost as 1 y(depth), color(depth) on a zone, label(depth) Polar, Naming the nodes
degree layout the number of rows that name the node size(degree), color(degree), label(degree) Network
distance path * cluster the distance at which each pair of branches joins y(distance), or x(distance) for a tree drawn sideways; both may be left out Cluster

These names are checked too. Write another name, and gog refuses the sentence and says which name to use:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + y(n) + text * flow(class, survived) + label(slot)
data(titanic) + y(col.n) + text * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + label(col.slot)
data(titanic) + y(:n) + text * flow(:class, :survived) + label(:slot)
plot(data(titanic), y(col.n), layer(text, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  label(col.slot))
Error:
! gog: under `flow` a `text` names the slots, and the flow publishes each slot's name under `name` — write `label(name)`, not `label(slot)`.
gog: `label(slot)` refers to a column that is not in the data. Check the spelling of `slot`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A column that a transform writes can also be named on other channels. Each channel checks it by the same rules it uses for a column of your table. The count that point * count puts on y can also size each point, so the larger points are the continents with more countries:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(continent) + size(count)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(col.continent) + size(col.count)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(:continent) + size(:count)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count), x(col.continent),
  size(col.count))

“Given gapminder 2007: points derived by count, x is continent, size by count.”

A cluster tree takes color(distance) the same way (Cluster). On label, a text layer prints the count on each bar, as Text shows. A zone’s color takes a continuous column, so color(count) draws a heatmap, as the table of columns at the start of this section shows. A bar’s color needs a categorical column, and count is continuous, so this sentence is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + color(count)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + color(col.count)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + color(:count)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  color(col.count))
Error:
! gog: `color(count)` names the `count` that `bar * count` writes, a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `bar` needs a categorical (text) column. Use `opacity` to show a numeric column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To color the bars, name a categorical column, such as color(continent). To show each bar’s count by how faint it is, write opacity(count), the channel the message names. opacity takes a continuous column, so the count is accepted. Oceania, with two countries, has the faintest bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + opacity(count)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + opacity(col.count)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + opacity(:count)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  opacity(col.count))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, opacity by count.”

Here the opacity repeats what the height already shows. The example shows only that opacity accepts a column that a transform writes, just as it accepts a column of your table.

Some sentences that name a column a transform writes are valid grammar that gog does not draw yet. One is a sunburst with color(name), which would give each node a color of its own. gog refuses it and draws nothing, and the message asks you to leave that color() out. confidence, deviation, smooth_band and straight_band write one more column, center. An interval draws it for you, as a dot. gog does not yet draw center on any channel, so a sentence that names it on one is refused.

25.25.3 Your table’s columns after a transform

You may want a plot of counts to show one more column of your table, such as gdp on size. A statistic such as count or mean replaces your rows with new ones, so that column may no longer be there. After bar * count there is one row for each bar, and every channel of that layer reads those rows.

Your table may already have a column with the same name as one a transform writes. A table of counts often has a count column, and a table of people often has a name column. The name in your sentence still means the column the transform writes, because the new rows do not hold your count column. So bar * count + y(count) draws the transform’s counts, and gog prints a message that says which count it drew. If your count column already holds counts, add them up instead with bar * sum + y(count). The message gives that sentence too.

Such a sentence is refused in one case: when another channel reads your table’s column of that name. In bar * count + x(count) + y(count), x(count) reads your column and y(count) names the transform’s, so one name would mean two columns. Rename your table’s column, or leave out y(count), since bar * count writes y itself.

The new rows also lack most other columns of your table, such as gdp. After point * count + x(continent) there is one row for each continent, and those rows have no gdp. So a sentence that sizes the points by gdp is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(continent) + size(gdp)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(col.continent) + size(col.gdp)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(:continent) + size(:gdp)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count), x(col.continent),
  size(col.gdp))
Error:
! gog: `size(gdp)` names a column of your table, and `point * count` replaces your rows with its own, one for each `continent`, which have no `gdp`. To show `gdp`, make a table with one row for each `continent`, holding its count and a summary of `gdp`. Draw that table with `point`, without `count`, and put the count on `y`. Otherwise, leave `size(gdp)` out.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

To size each point by its continent’s mean gdp, make a new table in the host language, as the message describes. Give it one row for each continent, with its number of countries and its mean gdp. Data makes the same counts with a database query. This book has made the table for you as continents_2007:

continents_2007: all 5 rows
continent countries mean_gdp
Asia 33 12473
Europe 30 25054
Africa 52 3089
Americas 25 11003
Oceania 2 29810

Draw it with point and without count, because the table already holds the counts, and put its countries column on y:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(continents_2007) + point + x(continent) + y(countries) + size(mean_gdp)
data(continents_2007) + point + x(col.continent) + y(col.countries) + size(col.mean_gdp)
data(continents_2007) + point + x(:continent) + y(:countries) +
  size(:mean_gdp)
plot(data(continents_2007), point, x(col.continent), y(col.countries),
  size(col.mean_gdp))

“Given the continents in 2007: points, x is continent, y is countries, size by mean gdp.”

Here the height shows the count and the size shows the mean gdp. Africa has the most countries and the smallest point, and Oceania has two countries and the largest.

Some statistics get different advice: the ones that fit a curve, such as smooth, and the ones that compute a low and a high value, such as range. For line * smooth + color(population), the message says to draw your rows in a layer of their own. The points below are your rows, so size(population) reads them. line * smooth has no size, and it fits its curve through the same points:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + x(gdp) + y(life) + point + size(population) +
  line * smooth
(data(gapminder_2007) + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + point + size(col.population) +
  line * smooth)
data(gapminder_2007) + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + point + size(:population) +
  line * smooth
plot(data(gapminder_2007), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), point,
  size(col.population), layer(line, smooth))

“Given gapminder 2007: x is gdp, y is life, points sized by population, and also a line derived by smooth.”

Not every column of your table is lost. Besides the positions a statistic groups by, two kinds of column are still on the new rows. One is a categorical column on a channel that splits the rows, such as color. The statistic runs within each group, so each new row keeps its group and is drawn in that group’s color. The other is the column a statistic reads. Under point * mean + x(continent) + y(life), size(life) sizes each point by its continent’s mean life.

order() cannot read gdp after bar * count either. There, order() ranks each continent by how many rows it has and reads no column of your table. So order(gdp) would name gdp but sort the bars by their counts, and gog refuses it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) + order(gdp, desc = TRUE)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) + order(col.gdp, desc = True)
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) +
  order(:gdp, desc = true)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  order(col.gdp, { desc: true }))
Error:
! gog: `order(gdp)` would never read `gdp`. `bar * count` measures each category of `continent` by how many rows it has and reads no column, so the categories would be sorted by that number. To sort them that way, write `order(count)`. To sort by `gdp`, draw it: `bar * mean + y(gdp) + order(gdp)` ranks each category by its mean `gdp`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

The message gives two sentences that draw. order(count) sorts the bars by their counts. bar * mean + y(gdp) + order(gdp) draws each continent’s mean gdp and sorts by it.

A column that a transform writes has the opposite limit. Four atoms read your table’s rows before any transform runs. group and play split them, a facet splits them into panels, and brush selects them. None of the four can name a column that a transform writes, because the column does not exist yet. color is not one of the four. It splits the rows only by a category of your table, and given the count, as in point * count + color(count), it reads the new rows. A sentence that names a written column in one of the four is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(continent) + play(count)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(col.continent) + play(col.count)
data(gapminder_2007) + point * count + x(:continent) + play(:count)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(point, count), x(col.continent),
  play(col.count))
Error:
! gog: `play(count)` names the `count` that `point * count` writes, but `play` cuts the table's rows into frames before any transform runs, so there is no `count` yet to cut by. Name a column of the table: `play(<column>)`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

play() needs a column of your table instead. Play counts the countries in each continent and plays them by year, a column of its table.

25.25.4 What each statistic reads and writes

The eighteen transforms in the table at the start of this chapter each write their answer into a named column. This table lists the column each one reads and the column it writes.

Transform Reads from Writes to
bin x(column) x(column) (bin centers), y(count) (counts)
count x(column) x(column) (unique values), y(count) (counts)
proportion the measurement before it, or x(column) if there is none y(proportion) (shares, summing to 1); after a statistic that reads y(column), such as sum, also y(proportion), while that y(column) keeps the statistic’s values
cumulative the measurement before it, or y(column) if there is none y(cumulative) (the running totals), while the measurement keeps each position’s own value
smooth x(column), y(column) same x, same y (smoothed values)
straight x(column), y(column) same x (100 positions along the line), same y (fitted values)
density x(column) x(column) (the points where the curve is estimated), y(density) (density)
sum / mean / median / max / min / quantile x(column), y(column) x(column) (unique), y(column) (aggregated)
range x(column), y(column) x(column) (each group twice), y(column) (low, then high)
confidence x(column), y(column) x(column) (each group twice), y(column) (low, then high), center (the mean)
deviation x(column), y(column) x(column) (each group twice), y(column) (low, then high), center (the mean)
smooth_band x(column), y(column) x(column) (100 positions along the curve, each twice), y(column) (low, then high), center (the fitted value)
straight_band x(column), y(column) x(column) (100 positions along the line, each twice), y(column) (low, then high), center (the fitted value)

One row of that table changes when bin is composed with another statistic (see Chaining transforms). Cutting is then all it does. It writes the bin centers to x(column) as before and does not change y(column), so the statistic can reduce it. The y column then holds your column’s summary rather than a count.

25.26 In short

The counting transforms and proportion name the measurement they write, so y() uses that name or is left out. The reading transforms refuse without the column they read. A statistic runs inside each group, so binding color changes what it computes. Two transforms compose when their jobs differ and contradict when they do not. Four more transforms compute a whole picture, and four move overlapping marks. Some transforms write columns a sentence can name, and a statistic replaces your rows.

25.27 What comes next

A transform changes the values of one mark and no other. Operators says how whole sentences join: how two marks share a panel, and how one plot is split or set beside another.
